bdm-w1-q1.question: Fictional 'Sutra Stores' has one empty shelf. There are three options: snacks (₹12,000 profit per month), stationery (₹9,000 per month) or phone accessories (₹15,000 per month). The store picks phone accessories. What is the opportunity cost of this choice?
bdm-w1-q1.explanation: Opportunity cost is only the value of the next best alternative. After phone accessories, the best option is snacks (₹12,000), so option B is correct. Option A (₹12,000 + ₹9,000) is the trap of adding all the forgone options; the shelf could never have held both at once. Option D is the chosen option's own profit, not a cost.

bdm-w1-q2.question: Fictional 'Megha Foods' has already spent ₹4 lakh on market research for a new snack; this money will not come back in any case. It now has to decide whether to launch the snack. How should the ₹4 lakh be treated in this decision?
options: Add it to the expected cost of the launch
Launch for sure, otherwise the ₹4 lakh is wasted
Launch only if the expected profit can first recover the ₹4 lakh
Ignore it; compare only the future revenue and cost that the launch brings
bdm-w1-q2.explanation: The ₹4 lakh is a sunk cost: launch or no launch, it does not come back, so it is the same under both choices and cannot change the decision. Option D is correct. Options B and C are two forms of the sunk cost fallacy (changing the decision to 'save' or 'recover' the money). Option A mistakes it for a future cost.

bdm-w1-q3.question: Fictional factory 'Ankur Plastics' has the option of one overtime shift: it would make 500 extra bottles that sell at ₹40 each. Material cost is ₹22 per bottle and the shift needs ₹6,000 of overtime wages. The factory's monthly rent of ₹50,000 is already fixed. By how much does profit rise because of the overtime shift?
bdm-w1-q3.explanation: Incremental revenue = 500 × ₹40 = ₹20,000. Incremental cost = 500 × ₹22 + ₹6,000 = ₹17,000. Profit rises by ₹3,000, option A. Rent is the same whether or not the shift runs, so it is irrelevant; subtracting it gives option C (−₹47,000). Option B is the trap of forgetting overtime wages, and option D of forgetting material cost.

bdm-w1-q4.question: Fictional 'Rasta Couriers' makes 1,000 deliveries a month; total cost is ₹60,000 (an average of ₹60 per delivery). The analyst's cost model says total cost at 1,100 deliveries will be ₹64,500. A B2B client wants 100 extra deliveries at ₹50 each, with no effect on the rest of the business. What is the right decision?
options: Reject; ₹50 is below the ₹60 average cost, a ₹10 loss per delivery
Reject; this order makes a total loss of ₹1,000
Accept; the marginal cost of an extra delivery is ₹45, so profit rises by ₹500
bdm-w1-q4.explanation: Marginal cost = (₹64,500 − ₹60,000) ÷ 100 = ₹45 per delivery. Extra revenue ₹5,000 − extra cost ₹4,500 = ₹500 profit, so option C. Options A and B are the trap of comparing with the average cost (₹60); the fixed cost is already incurred, and the extra order only has to cover its own extra cost. Option D ignores the extra cost altogether.

bdm-w1-q5.question: In one zone of fictional grocery app 'Jaldi Mart', monthly contribution by number of delivery riders (₹ thousand) is: 1 rider: 40, 2 riders: 75, 3 riders: 100, 4 riders: 115, 5 riders: 125. Each rider costs ₹18 thousand a month. How many riders maximise profit?
bdm-w1-q5.explanation: Marginal contribution: 40, 35, 25, 15, 10 (₹ thousand). Keep adding riders while MB ≥ MC (18). The third rider's MB is 25 > 18 and the fourth's is 15 < 18, so 3 riders, option D. Check: profit = 22, 39, 46, 43, 35, highest at 3. Option A is the trap of maximising total contribution (forgetting cost). Option B is the mistake of thinking 'the first rider has the highest return, so stop there'.

bdm-w1-q6.question: Fictional fashion brand 'Rang Rasiya' had a season's kurtas made for ₹2,00,000 and they did not sell. There are now two options: (i) sell them as they are to an outlet for ₹90,000, or (ii) spend ₹40,000 on a redesign (rework) and sell them for ₹1,50,000. What is the right decision and why?
options: Rework; it earns ₹20,000 more than selling as-is
Sell as-is; spending another ₹40,000 on rework is throwing good money after bad
Rework; it earns ₹60,000 more than selling as-is
No difference; the ₹2,00,000 is lost either way
bdm-w1-q6.explanation: The ₹2,00,000 is sunk and the same under both options. Incremental comparison: rework nets ₹1,50,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹1,10,000; as-is gives ₹90,000. Rework is better by ₹20,000, option A. Option C forgets to subtract the rework cost (₹1,50,000 − ₹90,000). Option D correctly sees that ₹2,00,000 is sunk but then forgets to compare the future cash flows. Option B treats any extra spending as bad without looking at its incremental return.

bdm-w2-q1.question: The price of mobile data packs falls sharply. What happens in the market for OTT streaming subscriptions (used together with data, i.e. a complement)?
options: The streaming demand curve shifts left
The streaming supply curve shifts right
The streaming demand curve shifts right
There is a movement down along the streaming demand curve
bdm-w2-q1.explanation: When a complement (data) gets cheaper, more people subscribe at every streaming price, so the streaming demand curve shifts right, option C. Option D is the trap: a movement along the curve happens only when streaming's own price changes. Option A is what happens with substitutes. Data prices have no direct effect on the supply side (option B).

bdm-w2-q2.question: From sales data an analyst sees that when fictional tea brand 'Pahadi Leaf' raised its price by 10%, sales of competing brand 'Neel Giri' rose by 6% (everything else unchanged). What is the cross-price elasticity, and how are the two brands related?
bdm-w2-q2.explanation: Cross-price elasticity = %ΔQ(Neel Giri) ÷ %ΔP(Pahadi Leaf) = +6% ÷ +10% = +0.6. A positive sign means substitutes, option A. Option D is the trap of inverting the ratio (10 ÷ 6). Option C has the right number but misreads the sign; complements would have a negative sign.

bdm-w2-q3.question: In a fictional city market, demand for a cooking-gas accessory is Qd = 900 − 15P and supply is Qs = 25P − 300 (P in ₹). A large platform caps the price at ₹24. What happens in the market at this price?
bdm-w2-q3.explanation: Equilibrium: 900 − 15P = 25P − 300 ⇒ P = 30, Q = 450. ₹24 is below equilibrium, so Qd = 900 − 360 = 540 and Qs = 600 − 300 = 300; shortage = 540 − 300 = 240, option D. Option B (540 − 450) and option C (450 − 300) are both the trap of comparing with the equilibrium quantity; a shortage is the gap between Qd and Qs. Option A treats the cap as a floor.

bdm-w2-q4.question: Fictional 'Chhaya Umbrellas' has estimated demand Q = 1,200 − 40P. The current price is ₹18. What is the point elasticity at this price, and what does it imply for pricing?
options: |e| = 0.67, inelastic; a price cut will reduce revenue
|e| = 1.5, elastic; a small price cut will raise revenue
|e| = 1.5, elastic; a price rise will raise revenue
|e| = 1, unit elastic; a small price change will not change revenue
bdm-w2-q4.explanation: Q = 1,200 − 40 × 18 = 480. e = −40 × 18 ÷ 480 = −1.5, so |e| = 1.5, elastic. In the elastic range a price cut raises quantity proportionally more, so revenue rises, option B. Option C gets the elasticity right but applies the revenue rule backwards. Option A is the trap of inverting the ratio (480 ÷ (40 × 18)).

bdm-w2-q5.question: Fictional ed-tech app 'Vidya Plus' ran an A/B price test: 5,000 subscriptions at ₹199 per month and 4,200 at ₹249. Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity (absolute value), and what happened to revenue?
bdm-w2-q5.explanation: %ΔQ = −800 ÷ 4,600 = −17.4%; %ΔP = 50 ÷ 224 = 22.3%; |e| = 17.4 ÷ 22.3 ≈ 0.78 (inelastic). Revenue went from ₹9,95,000 to ₹10,45,800, so it rose, option A. Option B is the result of simple % changes from the base values (16% ÷ 25.1%). Option C is the inverted ratio. Option D keeps the right elasticity but gets the revenue effect of a price rise under inelastic demand backwards.

bdm-w2-q6.question: According to fictional bakery chain 'Mithas', the weekly demand for a cake is linear: 1,100 units sell at ₹30 and 800 units at ₹45. At what price is weekly revenue highest?
bdm-w2-q6.explanation: Slope b = (1,100 − 800) ÷ (45 − 30) = 20 units per ₹. Q = 1,100 − 20(P − 30) = 1,700 − 20P. Revenue peaks at P = a ÷ 2b = 1,700 ÷ 40 = ₹42.50 (Q = 850, revenue ₹36,125), option D. Option B is the choke price (Q = 0), where revenue is zero. Options A and C are the trap of picking the better of the two given data points; revenue at ₹45 is ₹36,000, less than ₹36,125.

bdm-w3-q1.question: The ERP of fictional factory 'Vega Auto Parts' automatically reorders the same grade of lubricant oil from the same supplier every month, without any review. Which buying situation is this?
bdm-w3-q1.explanation: Same item, same supplier, routine reorder without review: straight rebuy, option A. Option B would apply if a change in specs, price or supplier were being considered. Option C is a first-time purchase. Option D means buying a whole integrated solution from one supplier, which is not the case here.

bdm-w3-q2.question: 20 rooms at fictional hotel 'Sagar Inn' stayed empty tonight. Tomorrow it is impossible to sell these rooms for 'tonight'. Which property of services is shown here?
bdm-w3-q2.explanation: A service cannot be stored: tonight's unused capacity is gone for good. This is perishability, option C, and it is why hotels use dynamic pricing and overbooking. Option A (cannot be touched) and option D (variation in quality) are also properties of services, but they do not describe this situation.

bdm-w3-q3.question: At fictional company 'Lohit Steel', an executive in the purchase department decides which vendors' brochures, emails and meeting requests reach the engineering team and which do not. What is this person's role in the buying centre?
bdm-w3-q3.explanation: A person who controls the flow of information and vendor access to the buying team is the gatekeeper, option B. An influencer (option A) gives input on specs or evaluation, like engineers or the IT head; here the executive is not evaluating anything, only blocking or passing things on. The decider makes the final choice and the user uses the product.

bdm-w3-q4.question: A fictional distributor always keeps inventory equal to 2 months of sales (sales = last month's sales). Last month sales were 1,000 units, inventory was 2,000 units, and it ordered 1,000 units every month. This month sales rose 10% to 1,100. How much will the distributor order from the manufacturer this month?
bdm-w3-q4.explanation: Order = replacement of units sold + change in the inventory target. The target inventory is 2 × 1,100 = 2,200, up by 200. Order = 1,100 + 200 = 1,300, which is 30% above 1,000, option D. Consumer demand rose 10% but the manufacturer's orders rose 30%: this is the bullwhip effect. Option A forgets the inventory adjustment; option C mistakes the new inventory target for the order.

bdm-w3-q5.question: A salesperson for predictive-maintenance software asks a plant manager: "If these unplanned breakdowns keep happening twice a month, what will that do to your delivery penalties and overtime costs?" In the SPIN model, what type of question is this?
bdm-w3-q5.explanation: The problem (breakdowns) is already known; this question explores its business consequences (penalties, overtime), so it is an implication question, option B. Option D is the trap: a problem question looks for the pain point ("do the machines stop unexpectedly?"). A need-payoff question (option C) asks for the value of a solution ("how much would you save if breakdowns halved?").

bdm-w3-q6.question: One B2B account of fictional packaging supplier 'Patra Packs' brings ₹3 lakh of margin every year. The first year's margin is certain; after that, each year the account stays with probability 80% (given it stayed the year before). Ignoring discounting, what is the expected total margin from this account?
bdm-w3-q6.explanation: Expected margin = 3 × (1 + 0.8 + 0.8² + ...) = 3 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = ₹15 lakh, option C (an expected relationship of 5 years). Option B (3 × 0.8 ÷ 0.2) leaves out the certain first-year margin. Option D (3 ÷ 0.8) applies retention the wrong way, and option A is only the second year's expected margin (3 × 0.8).

bdm-w4-q1.question: Cell E1 holds the GST rate. Cell C2 contains the formula `=B2*$E$1`. The formula is copied down from C2 to C5. What is the formula in C5?
bdm-w4-q1.explanation: Copying down 3 rows changes the relative reference B2 to B5, while `$E$1` is absolute and stays fixed: `=B5*$E$1`, option D. Option A is what you would get without the `$` (E1 would also shift to E4). Option C is the trap of thinking the row still moves after a `$`.

bdm-w4-q2.question: Range B2:B8 holds the order values 450, 1200, 500, 75, 980, 500, 620. What does `=COUNTIF(B2:B8, ">=500")` return?
bdm-w4-q2.explanation: Values of 500 or more: 1200, 500, 980, 500, 620, i.e. 5, option B. COUNTIF counts every cell separately, so both 500s count; counting them once gives option C (4). Option A (3) is the result of `">500"`, which drops the boundary value.

bdm-w4-q3.question: In a price-volume grid, cell B2 contains `=$A2*B$1` (quantities in column A, prices in row 1). The formula is copied from B2 to D4. What is the formula in D4?
bdm-w4-q3.explanation: B2 to D4 is 2 columns right and 2 rows down. In `$A2` column A is locked and the row moves: `$A4`. In `B$1` row 1 is locked and the column moves: `D$1`. The result is `=$A4*D$1`, option C. Option A forgets the row shift, option D the column shift; option B ignores the `$` signs and shifts everything.

bdm-w4-q4.question: A fictional distributor's discount slab table is in G2:H5 in ascending order (see the code). For an order value of ₹30,000, what does `=VLOOKUP(30000, G2:H5, 2, TRUE)` return?
bdm-w4-q4.explanation: TRUE means approximate match: in sorted column G the largest value less than or equal to 30000 is 25000, so that row's 8% is returned, option A. Option B is the trap of thinking the next (higher) slab is picked. Option C would be the result of an exact match (FALSE), since 30000 is not in the table.

bdm-w4-q5.question: On fictional 'Disha Electricals' sheet (see the code), what does `=SUMIFS(D2:D9, B2:B9, "West", D2:D9, ">5000")` return?
bdm-w4-q5.explanation: Both conditions together: Region is West AND Amount > 5000. West rows: 7200, 4800, 5000, 6300, 5600; of these > 5000: 7200 + 6300 + 5600 = 19100, option C. Option B also counts 5000 (as if `">=5000"`). Option A applies only the West condition, and option D only the amount condition.

bdm-w4-q6.question: On the sheet below, what does `=INDEX(B2:D6, MATCH(MAX(D2:D6), D2:D6, 0), 2)` return?
bdm-w4-q6.explanation: MAX(D2:D6) = 58000. MATCH(..., 0) returns the FIRST position of an exact match: in D2:D6, 58000 first appears at position 2 (row 3). INDEX(B2:D6, 2, 2) = second column of range B:D (column C) in the second row: 'South', option B. Option A is the trap of counting columns from A instead of B, option C of thinking the last match (Charu) is picked, and option D of taking column 3.

bdm-w5-q1.question: Which one of these balance sheet items of a fictional company is a liability?
bdm-w5-q1.explanation: Unearned revenue is a customer's advance for which goods or services are still owed, a present obligation: a liability, option B. Option C is the trap: with prepaid rent the company has paid in advance, so the future benefit is its own and it is an asset. Receivables and inventory are also assets.

bdm-w5-q2.question: Fictional company 'Bansi Foods' has annual revenue of ₹80 lakh and expenses of ₹62 lakh. During the year it paid ₹5 lakh of dividends to shareholders. A dashboard shows 'net profit ₹13 lakh'. Which statement is correct?
options: Net profit is ₹18 lakh; a dividend is a distribution of profit, not an expense
Net profit of ₹13 lakh is right; a dividend is also an expense
Net profit is ₹23 lakh; dividends are added to profit
Net profit is ₹18 lakh, and retained earnings also rise by ₹18 lakh
bdm-w5-q2.explanation: Net profit = ₹80 lakh − ₹62 lakh = ₹18 lakh, option A. A dividend does not appear in the income statement; it is deducted from retained earnings. Option D is half right, but retained earnings rise by ₹18 lakh − ₹5 lakh = ₹13 lakh, not ₹18 lakh. Option B is the dashboard's mistake.

bdm-w5-q3.question: On 1 November 2025, fictional SaaS startup 'Megh Cloud' received ₹2,40,000 upfront from a customer for a 12-month subscription. The financial year ends on 31 March 2026. What are the FY 2025-26 revenue and the deferred revenue on 31 March 2026?
bdm-w5-q3.explanation: Monthly revenue is ₹20,000. November to March is 5 months, so revenue is ₹1,00,000 and the obligation for the remaining 7 months, ₹1,40,000, is deferred revenue, option D. Option C swaps the two numbers. Option B counts 6 months, and option A treats the cash as revenue.

bdm-w5-q4.question: Fictional marketplace 'Haat Bazaar' sells goods on behalf of sellers (the sellers own the inventory; Haat Bazaar is an agent). Annual GMV is ₹50 crore, Haat Bazaar takes a 12% commission, and it also charges customers ₹1.5 crore of delivery fees. What is Haat Bazaar's revenue?
bdm-w5-q4.explanation: An agent's revenue is only what it earns for itself: commission 12% × ₹50 crore = ₹6 crore, plus delivery fees of ₹1.5 crore = ₹7.5 crore, option C. Options A and B are the trap of treating GMV as revenue; the sellers' share is their revenue. Option D forgets the delivery fees.

bdm-w5-q5.question: On 1 April, fictional company 'Tara Logistics' bought servers for ₹12 lakh (useful life 4 years, zero residual value, straight-line depreciation). The analyst's cost dashboard showed the full ₹12 lakh as this year's expense. What is the effect of this error on this year's profit?
options: Profit is shown ₹9 lakh too low (understated)
Profit is shown ₹12 lakh too low
Profit is shown ₹3 lakh too low
Profit is shown ₹9 lakh too high (overstated)
bdm-w5-q5.explanation: The correct expense is only this year's depreciation: ₹12 lakh ÷ 4 = ₹3 lakh. The dashboard deducted ₹12 lakh, i.e. ₹9 lakh of extra expense, so profit is understated by ₹9 lakh, option A. Option B forgets depreciation, option C takes the depreciation itself as the error, and option D gets the direction backwards.

bdm-w5-q6.question: At the start, fictional firm 'Kalp Consulting' has Assets ₹50 lakh = Liabilities ₹20 lakh + Equity ₹30 lakh. Then: (i) a client pays a ₹6 lakh advance for next year's service; (ii) it buys equipment for ₹8 lakh, ₹3 lakh in cash and the rest on credit; (iii) it delivers ₹10 lakh of service, invoice still unpaid; (iv) it pays a ₹2 lakh dividend in cash; (v) it pays this year's salaries of ₹4 lakh in cash. What are total assets and equity now?
bdm-w5-q6.explanation: Assets: 50 + 6 (cash) + 8 − 3 (equipment in, cash out) + 10 (receivable) − 2 − 4 = ₹65 lakh. Liabilities: 20 + 6 (deferred revenue) + 5 (equipment payable) = ₹31 lakh. Equity: 30 + 10 − 2 − 4 = ₹34 lakh; check 31 + 34 = 65, option D. Option A treats the advance as revenue (equity 40). Option C ignores the dividend. Option B records only the cash part of the equipment.

bdm-w6-q1.question: Fictional shop 'Gulmohar Crockery' bought ₹75,000 of goods from a supplier on credit. What is the correct journal entry?
bdm-w6-q1.explanation: Inventory (an asset) rises, so debit; the supplier must be paid, so a liability rises, so credit: option C. Option B is the entry for a cash purchase; no cash has left yet. Option A reverses the sides, and option D shows cash coming in, which never happened.

bdm-w6-q2.question: A fictional company records ₹5 lakh of depreciation on machines this year. Ignore tax. What is the effect of this depreciation entry on this year's cash?
options: A ₹5 lakh outflow appears in investing activities
No direct effect on cash; it is a non-cash expense
bdm-w6-q2.explanation: Depreciation only turns the machine's cost into expense over the years; no cash moves in this entry, option D. The cash left in investing activities when the machine was bought. Option B comes from depreciation being 'added back' in the indirect method, but the add-back only removes a non-cash expense; it does not create cash.

bdm-w6-q3.question: Fictional retailer 'Prism Optics' had opening inventory of 200 frames @ ₹300 and then bought 300 frames @ ₹340. During the period 350 frames sold at ₹500 each. What is the gross profit under the weighted average (periodic) method?
bdm-w6-q3.explanation: Average cost = (200 × 300 + 300 × 340) ÷ 500 = ₹324. COGS = 350 × 324 = ₹1,13,400. Revenue = 350 × 500 = ₹1,75,000. Gross profit = ₹61,600, option B. Option A is the FIFO answer (COGS ₹1,11,000). Option C costs every unit at the latest price of ₹340. Option D is the value of closing inventory (150 × 324), not profit.

bdm-w6-q4.question: At the start of the year a fictional company bought a machine for ₹8 lakh (life 5 years, zero residual). For the first year compare two options: SLM, or 30% WDV. What difference does this make to first-year EBIT and EBITDA?
options: EBIT is ₹80,000 higher under SLM; EBITDA is the same under both
EBIT is ₹80,000 higher under WDV; EBITDA is the same under both
EBIT is ₹80,000 higher under SLM, and EBITDA is also ₹80,000 higher
No difference, because total depreciation over the whole life is the same
bdm-w6-q4.explanation: SLM depreciation = 8,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹1,60,000; WDV = 30% × 8,00,000 = ₹2,40,000. SLM has ₹80,000 less expense, so EBIT is ₹80,000 higher, option A. EBITDA is measured before depreciation, so it is the same under both methods; option C forgets this. Option D is right that total depreciation over the whole life is equal, but the year-by-year timing differs.

bdm-w6-q5.question: A fictional wholesaler sold goods costing ₹60,000 for ₹90,000 on credit. What is the effect of this one transaction?
options: Revenue rises by ₹90,000 and cash rises by ₹90,000
Profit rises by ₹30,000, receivables rise by ₹90,000, inventory falls by ₹60,000, cash is unchanged
Profit rises by ₹90,000 and receivables rise by ₹90,000
Profit rises by ₹30,000 and cash rises by ₹30,000
bdm-w6-q5.explanation: Revenue ₹90,000 − COGS ₹60,000 = profit ₹30,000. No money has come in yet, so receivables rise by ₹90,000 and cash is unchanged; goods left, so inventory falls by ₹60,000. The net change in assets, +₹30,000, equals the change in equity: option B. Options A and D treat a credit sale as cash; option C forgets COGS.

bdm-w6-q6.question: Fictional company 'Indus Tiles' has opening cash of ₹5 lakh. During the year: net profit ₹8 lakh; depreciation ₹2 lakh; trade receivables rose by ₹3 lakh; trade payables rose by ₹1 lakh; it bought a ₹6 lakh machine for cash; it repaid ₹1 lakh of loan; it paid a ₹2 lakh dividend. What is closing cash?
bdm-w6-q6.explanation: CFO = 8 + 2 − 3 + 1 = ₹8 lakh. CFI = −₹6 lakh. CFF = −1 − 2 = −₹3 lakh. Closing cash = 5 + 8 − 6 − 3 = ₹4 lakh, option C. Option A forgets to add back depreciation. Option B adds the rise in receivables (wrong sign). Option D does not treat the dividend as a cash outflow.

bdm-w7-q1.question: Fictional listed company 'Avani Cements' has PAT of ₹48 crore and 2 crore equity shares (no preference shares). The share price is ₹360. What is the P/E ratio?
bdm-w7-q1.explanation: EPS = 48 ÷ 2 = ₹24. P/E = 360 ÷ 24 = 15, option A. Option B is the trap of dividing the price by total PAT (₹48 crore); P/E is a per-share ratio. Option C is the EPS itself, and option D is the inverse ratio (EPS ÷ price), the earnings yield.

bdm-w7-q2.question: In which pair do both ratios measure solvency (long-term leverage and debt servicing)?
options: Debt-equity ratio and interest coverage ratio
bdm-w7-q2.explanation: Debt-equity shows the share of debt in the capital structure and interest coverage shows how many times earnings cover interest: both are solvency ratios, option B. Option A lists liquidity (short-term) ratios; this is the common trap because both are about 'ability to pay'. Option C lists efficiency ratios and option D market valuation ratios.

bdm-w7-q3.question: Fictional company 'Kiran Pharma' has EPS of ₹15, paid a dividend of ₹6 per share, and its share price is ₹240. What are the dividend yield and the payout ratio?
bdm-w7-q3.explanation: Dividend yield = DPS ÷ price = 6 ÷ 240 = 2.5%. Payout = DPS ÷ EPS = 6 ÷ 15 = 40%. Option D. Option B's 6.25% is the earnings yield (15 ÷ 240), not the dividend yield. Option A swaps the two labels, and option C computes payout upside down (EPS ÷ DPS).

bdm-w7-q4.question: Fictional distributor 'Sangam Traders' has revenue of ₹9 crore, average total assets of ₹6 crore and a net profit margin of 5%. What is ROA (PAT ÷ average total assets)?
bdm-w7-q4.explanation: Asset turnover = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5. ROA = net margin × asset turnover = 5% × 1.5 = 7.5% (PAT = ₹0.45 crore, ÷ ₹6 crore). Option C. Option A divides margin by turnover, option B takes the margin itself as ROA, and option D multiplies the margin by the asset figure (6).

bdm-w7-q5.question: Fictional company 'Sheetal Appliances' has total equity of ₹50 crore and 2 crore equity shares. The share price is ₹80. What is the price-to-book (P/B) ratio?
bdm-w7-q5.explanation: Book value per share = 50 ÷ 2 = ₹25. P/B = 80 ÷ 25 = 3.2, option D. Option A divides the price by total equity (₹50 crore), forgetting to go to the per-share level. Option B is the inverse ratio, and option C is just the BVPS.

bdm-w7-q6.question: Fictional company 'Orbit Telecom Services' has 1 crore shares trading at ₹150. Borrowings are ₹40 crore, cash and equivalents ₹10 crore, and EBITDA is ₹24 crore. What is EV/EBITDA?
bdm-w7-q6.explanation: Market cap = 1 crore × ₹150 = ₹150 crore. EV = 150 + 40 − 10 = ₹180 crore. EV/EBITDA = 180 ÷ 24 = 7.5, option A. Option B uses only market cap (150 ÷ 24). Option C adds cash instead of subtracting it (200 ÷ 24). Option D forgets debt (140 ÷ 24).

bdm-w8-q1.question: Fictional 'Shakti Home Appliances Ltd' had revenue of ₹400 crore in FY25 and ₹480 crore in FY26. What is the revenue growth?
bdm-w8-q1.explanation: Growth = (480 − 400) ÷ 400 = 80 ÷ 400 = 20%, option D. Option A is the trap of dividing by the new year (80 ÷ 480). Option B writes the absolute change (₹80 crore) as a %, and option C mistakes the ratio 480 ÷ 400 for growth.

bdm-w8-q2.question: The same company's FY26 revenue is ₹480 crore and COGS is ₹322 crore (FY25: revenue ₹400 crore, COGS ₹260 crore). What is the FY26 gross margin?
bdm-w8-q2.explanation: Gross margin = (480 − 322) ÷ 480 = 158 ÷ 480 = 32.9%, option C. Option A is COGS as a % (322 ÷ 480), not the margin. Option B is FY25's margin (140 ÷ 400), the wrong year. Option D divides gross profit by COGS (158 ÷ 322), which is the markup, not the margin.

bdm-w8-q3.question: Trade receivables of Shakti Home Appliances (fictional) were ₹60 crore at the end of FY25 and ₹90 crore at the end of FY26; FY26 revenue is ₹480 crore. What is FY26 DSO, using closing receivables and 365 days?
bdm-w8-q3.explanation: DSO = 90 ÷ 480 × 365 = 68.4 days, option A (FY25 was 54.75 days, so collection slowed by about 14 days). Option B is FY25's DSO. Option C is receivables turnover (480 ÷ 90 = 5.3 times), not days. Option D pairs FY25 receivables with FY26 revenue, a period mismatch.

bdm-w8-q4.question: Shakti Home Appliances (fictional) FY26: gross profit ₹158 crore, other opex ₹86 crore, depreciation ₹14 crore, interest ₹12 crore, tax 25%. FY25 interest coverage was 6.00. What is FY26 interest coverage (EBIT ÷ interest)?
bdm-w8-q4.explanation: EBIT = 158 − 86 − 14 = ₹58 crore. Coverage = 58 ÷ 12 = 4.83, weaker than FY25's 6.00, option B. Option C divides PBT (46) by interest; profit after interest is the wrong base for coverage. Option D uses PAT (34.5).

bdm-w8-q5.question: Shakti Home Appliances (fictional) has FY26 PAT of ₹34.5 crore and CFO of ₹8.5 crore. In FY25, CFO ÷ PAT was about 1. What is the best reading of FY26 CFO ÷ PAT?
options: About 0.25; a large part of profit is stuck in working capital (receivables, inventory), which questions earnings quality
About 4.06; cash generation is far above profit, a strong sign
About 0.25; this is normal because depreciation is non-cash
About 0.25; it means PAT was calculated wrongly
bdm-w8-q5.explanation: 8.5 ÷ 34.5 ≈ 0.25. The depreciation add-back pushes CFO ABOVE PAT, so a ratio this low comes from money stuck in working capital (receivables +30, inventory +15): option A. Option C gives the reason backwards. Option B is the inverse ratio (34.5 ÷ 8.5). Option D is a wrong conclusion: a low ratio does not prove fraud or error, it only raises questions.

bdm-w8-q6.question: FY26 data for Shakti Home Appliances (fictional) is below (₹ crore). Simplification: CFO = PAT + depreciation − change in net working capital. What are FY26 CFO and free cash flow (CFO − capex)?
bdm-w8-q6.explanation: Change in working capital = +30 (receivables) + 15 (inventory) − 5 (payables rose, saving cash) = 40. CFO = 34.5 + 14 − 40 = 8.5; FCF = 8.5 − 67 = −58.5, option C. Option A ignores working capital. Option D also subtracts the rise in payables (wrong sign, 50). Option B forgets the depreciation add-back.

bdm-w9-q1.question: Fictional company 'Sona Biscuits' makes only one product. What kind of cost is the wrapper (packaging material) used on every packet?
bdm-w9-q1.explanation: Wrapper cost rises with every packet (variable) and is traced straight to the product (direct): option B. Option C is the trap: direct does not mean fixed; direct/indirect is about traceability, fixed/variable about behaviour with volume. A cost like factory rent would be fixed and indirect.

bdm-w9-q2.question: Fictional 'Kanak Bags' sells a bag for ₹500; variable cost is ₹300 per bag and monthly fixed costs are ₹4,00,000. How many bags must it sell each month to break even?
bdm-w9-q2.explanation: CM = 500 − 300 = ₹200 per bag. Break-even = 4,00,000 ÷ 200 = 2,000 bags, option C (revenue ₹10 lakh). Option A divides fixed cost by price, as if the whole price went to fixed costs. Option B divides by the variable cost.

bdm-w9-q3.question: The electricity bill of fictional factory 'Shilpa Castings' was ₹58,000 in a month with 2,000 machine hours and ₹1,03,000 in a month with 5,000 machine hours (these are the lowest and highest activity months). Using the high-low method, what is the monthly fixed part?
bdm-w9-q3.explanation: Variable rate = (1,03,000 − 58,000) ÷ (5,000 − 2,000) = 45,000 ÷ 3,000 = ₹15 per hour. Fixed = 58,000 − 15 × 2,000 = ₹28,000 (check: 1,03,000 − 75,000 = ₹28,000), option A. Option B treats the low month's whole bill as fixed. Option C is the cost difference, which belongs to the variable part. Option D is the low month's variable part (15 × 2,000).

bdm-w9-q4.question: Fictional 'Arya Fitness Bands' has a price of ₹1,200, variable cost of ₹750 per unit and fixed costs of ₹9,00,000. How many units must it sell to earn a profit of ₹4,50,000?
bdm-w9-q4.explanation: CM = 1,200 − 750 = ₹450. Units = (9,00,000 + 4,50,000) ÷ 450 = 13,50,000 ÷ 450 = 3,000, option D. Option A is just break-even (target profit forgotten). Option B divides only the profit by CM (fixed cost forgotten). Option C divides by price instead of CM.

bdm-w9-q5.question: Fictional SaaS company 'Lekha Books' has total contribution of ₹30 lakh and operating profit (EBIT) of ₹6 lakh. With price, variable cost per unit and fixed costs unchanged, sales volume rises 10%. What is the new EBIT?
bdm-w9-q5.explanation: DOL = 30 ÷ 6 = 5. A 10% sales rise lifts EBIT by 5 × 10% = 50%: ₹9 lakh, option C. Direct check: contribution ₹33 lakh, fixed costs unchanged at ₹24 lakh, EBIT ₹9 lakh. Option A raises EBIT by only 10% (operating leverage forgotten). Option B is the new contribution, not EBIT.

bdm-w9-q6.question: Fictional 'Rasoi Appliances' sells two products in a sales mix of 3 mixers : 2 grinders. Mixer: price ₹400, variable cost ₹250. Grinder: price ₹600, variable cost ₹420. Monthly fixed costs are ₹8,10,000. At this mix, how many mixers and grinders must be sold to break even?
bdm-w9-q6.explanation: CM: mixer ₹150, grinder ₹180. CM of a bundle (3 mixers + 2 grinders) = 3 × 150 + 2 × 180 = ₹810. Bundles = 8,10,000 ÷ 810 = 1,000, i.e. 3,000 mixers and 2,000 grinders, option B. Option C uses the simple average of the two CMs (165), ignoring the 3:2 mix. Option A makes each product cover the whole fixed cost on its own. Option D mistakes 1,000 bundles for 1,000 units of each product.

bdm-w10-q1.question: A fictional CRM vendor's sales rep asks a lead whether budget is approved, who will make the final decision, what the problem is and by when a solution is needed. Which step of the selling process is this?
bdm-w10-q1.explanation: Checking Budget, Authority, Need and Timeline (BANT) qualifies the lead, which is part of the prospecting and qualifying step, option C. Option A is the trap because this is also an early conversation, but the goal of the approach is rapport and credibility, not filtering. Closing and follow-up come later.

bdm-w10-q2.question: A salesperson for fictional accounting software says: "This will save your finance team 6 hours of manual reconciliation every week." In the FAB framework, what is this statement?
bdm-w10-q2.explanation: It states a concrete gain for the customer (the team's time), so it is a benefit, option A. A feature is a property of the product ('automatic bank-feed matching') and an advantage is what the feature does ('entries match themselves'). Option C is the most common trap because advantage and benefit are close; the difference is that a benefit speaks of the customer's business result.

bdm-w10-q3.question: Last quarter, fictional HR-tech company 'Kaam Sathi' turned 1,500 leads into 300 qualified, 90 proposals and 30 wins. At the same conversion rates, how many leads are needed next quarter for 45 wins?
bdm-w10-q3.explanation: Overall lead-to-win = 30 ÷ 1,500 = 2%. Leads = 45 ÷ 0.02 = 2,250, option B (stage by stage: 45 ÷ (30/90) = 135 proposals, 135 ÷ 0.3 = 450 qualified, 450 ÷ 0.2 = 2,250 leads). Option C adds just 15 leads for 15 extra wins, as if every lead won. Option D assumes 1% conversion. Option A stops the back-solve at the qualified stage: 450 qualified are needed, not leads.

bdm-w10-q4.question: Fictional 'Tarang Analytics' has this pipeline: 5 deals × ₹10 lakh in 'discovery' (probability 20%), 3 deals × ₹15 lakh in 'proposal' (50%), and 2 deals × ₹20 lakh in 'negotiation' (80%). What is the weighted pipeline?
bdm-w10-q4.explanation: Weighted = 50 × 0.2 + 45 × 0.5 + 40 × 0.8 = 10 + 22.5 + 32 = ₹64.5 lakh, option D. Option A is the unweighted total. Option B applies the simple average of the three probabilities (50%) to the whole pipeline, ignoring how the value is spread across stages. Option C counts only the negotiation deals, at full value.

bdm-w10-q5.question: A fictional manufacturer raises a price objection. The vendor's solution costs ₹30 lakh one-time plus ₹6 lakh a year of maintenance, and the customer's own data shows it will save ₹18 lakh a year. What payback period should be presented to handle the objection?
bdm-w10-q5.explanation: Net annual saving = 18 − 6 = ₹12 lakh. Payback = 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 years, option D. Option A forgets the maintenance cost (30 ÷ 18), which destroys credibility in front of the customer's finance team. Option B divides the one-time cost by the maintenance.

bdm-w10-q6.question: A sales team at fictional 'Nirmaan ERP' has a quarterly quota of ₹2 crore. The historical win rate (by value) is 25%. Open pipeline is currently ₹5.6 crore. How much more pipeline (value) is needed to make the quota realistic?
options: None; the pipeline is 2.8 times the quota
bdm-w10-q6.explanation: At a 25% win rate, winning ₹2 crore needs 2 ÷ 0.25 = ₹8 crore of pipeline (4× coverage). Gap = 8 − 5.6 = ₹2.4 crore, option A. Option C is the gap in expected bookings (5.6 × 0.25 = 1.4, 2 − 1.4 = 0.6), not in pipeline; ₹0.6 crore of bookings needs 0.6 ÷ 0.25 = ₹2.4 crore of pipeline. Option B judges coverage without the win rate. Option D just subtracts the quota from the pipeline.

bdm-w11-q1.question: What does BATNA correctly mean in a negotiation?
options: The best price you can get in this deal
The range between the two parties' reservation prices
An opening offer that works as an anchor
Your best alternative if this deal does not happen
bdm-w11-q1.explanation: BATNA = Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement, i.e. your best option if the deal fails, option D. The reservation price comes from it. Option B is the definition of ZOPA, a common confusion. Option A is a target or aspiration price, and option C is about anchoring.

bdm-w11-q2.question: Fictional delivery app 'Dabba Express' collected customers' phone numbers only to send delivery updates. Now, as part of a deal with a partner, the marketing team wants to send the partner's loan offers to these numbers without fresh consent. Which data protection principle is most directly broken?
bdm-w11-q2.explanation: The data was collected for a specific purpose (delivery updates); using it for a new, different purpose (a partner's loan offers) without consent breaks purpose limitation, option B. Option D (keeping data longer than needed) is also a principle, but the problem here is the purpose of use, not the duration. Accuracy and portability are not directly involved.

bdm-w11-q3.question: A software vendor opens the negotiation at a ₹90 lakh 'list price'. The buyer's team has benchmark data that such solutions sell for around ₹55 lakh, yet it counters at ₹75 lakh and is happy to close at ₹70 lakh, having 'saved ₹20 lakh'. Which negotiation trap did the buyer fall into?
bdm-w11-q3.explanation: The vendor's first number (₹90 lakh) became the reference point, and the buyer countered and measured 'savings' from it instead of from its own benchmark (₹55 lakh): anchoring, option C. Option A would apply if the buyer's first offer were accepted at once and it felt it had paid too much. Option B is staying stuck in a deal because of resources already committed, which is not shown here.

bdm-w11-q4.question: At fictional company 'Kriti Cosmetics', the Sales dashboard shows 1,200 'qualified leads' and the Marketing dashboard shows 1,850. Both teams say the metric is theirs. What is the best approach for the head of analytics?
options: Agree a written definition together with both teams, name one data owner, and keep the metric in one shared source of truth
Ask the CEO to choose one team's number and shut down the other team's dashboard
Leave both numbers on the dashboards so that neither team is upset
Make the average of the two (1,525) the official number
bdm-w11-q4.explanation: The gap usually comes from different definitions and sources; understanding both teams' needs and building a common definition, owner and single source of truth is the collaborating approach that fixes the root cause, option A. Option D is compromising but creates a number that matches no definition. Option C is avoiding (the confusion stays), and option B uses competing/authority and ignores one team's needs.

bdm-w11-q5.question: Fictional buyer 'Vardaan Hospitals' and supplier 'MedEquip' are negotiating two issues. The points for each option are below (higher = better). Which combination maximises the two parties' total points?
bdm-w11-q5.explanation: Totals: A = 40 + 20 = 60; B = 40 + 50 = 90; C = 10 + 50 = 60; D = 20 + 10 = 30. Option B is highest (90): delivery matters more to the buyer and payment terms to the supplier, so each party gives up its less important issue (logrolling). Option A is best for the buyer (60 points) but gives the supplier nothing; that is the fixed-pie trap.

bdm-w11-q6.question: Fictional vendor 'Prisma Data' has a delivery cost of ₹32 lakh on a project; if the deal fails, the same team can earn ₹10 lakh profit on another project. Buyer 'Unnati Retail' has a competitor's quote of ₹52 lakh, which needs another ₹3 lakh of switching cost (Prisma has no such cost). What is the ZOPA?
bdm-w11-q6.explanation: Seller's reservation price = 32 + 10 = ₹42 lakh (below that the other project is better). Buyer's reservation price = 52 + 3 = ₹55 lakh (the competitor's full cost). ZOPA = ₹42–55 lakh, option D. Option B forgets the buyer's switching cost; option C forgets the seller's forgone profit (opportunity cost); option A forgets both.

bdm-w12-q1.question: At fictional restaurant chain 'Zaika', when an order arrives wrong, the manager comes to the table, apologises politely, honestly explains the cause of the error and listens carefully to the customer. Which justice dimension does this part of the recovery address?
bdm-w12-q1.explanation: Politeness, empathy, a sincere apology and an explanation, i.e. how the customer is treated: interactional justice, option A. Option B would apply if an outcome were given (refund, free dish). Option C is the fairness and speed of the process. Option D is not a justice dimension at all but a possible result of recovery.

bdm-w12-q2.question: What is the most accurate meaning of the 'service recovery paradox'?
options: After a service failure, customers always switch
The bigger the compensation, the higher the loyalty, without any limit
Customers who do not complain are satisfied
After an excellent recovery, some customers' satisfaction can rise above the level it would have had with no failure
bdm-w12-q2.explanation: The paradox is that failure + excellent recovery sometimes gives higher satisfaction than no failure, option D; it is not guaranteed and does not work for repeated failures. Option B is the trap: compensation has limited effect, and process and behaviour also matter. Option C is the misunderstanding that the complaint iceberg warns against.

bdm-w12-q3.question: A B2B client of fictional cloud provider 'Akash Hosting' pays ₹6,00,000 per month. SLA: no credit at monthly uptime of 99.9% or more; 10% credit from 99.0% up to below 99.9%; 25% credit below 99.0%. In a 30-day month total downtime was 300 minutes. How much service credit does the client get?
bdm-w12-q3.explanation: The month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. Uptime = 1 − 300 ÷ 43,200 ≈ 99.31%, which is between 99.0% and 99.9%: 10% credit = ₹60,000, option C. Option D is the fee pro-rated for the downtime minutes, not the SLA slab. Option B applies the 25% slab (overestimating 300 minutes), and option A reads 99.31% as above 99.9%.

bdm-w12-q4.question: A new earphone model of fictional electronics brand 'Volt' got 120 complaints in a month. Industry research says only 4% of dissatisfied customers complain formally. What is the estimated number of dissatisfied customers of this model this month?
bdm-w12-q4.explanation: Complaints come from only 4% of dissatisfied customers: 120 ÷ 0.04 = 3,000 dissatisfied customers, option B. Option D (3,000 − 120) counts only those who did not complain, not all the dissatisfied. Option C is 120 × 4%, the calculation turned upside down. Option A merely adds 4% to 120 (120 × 1.04 ≈ 125).

bdm-w12-q5.question: On fictional food delivery app 'Thali Express', 300 orders a day arrive late or wrong. Without recovery, 25% of these customers churn; giving every affected customer an immediate apology + ₹100 voucher cuts churn to 10%. Average customer lifetime value (margin) is ₹3,000. Net of the voucher cost, how much expected loss does the recovery program save per day?
bdm-w12-q5.explanation: Without recovery: 300 × 25% × 3,000 = ₹2,25,000. With recovery: 300 × 10% × 3,000 = ₹90,000 churn loss + 300 × 100 = ₹30,000 vouchers = ₹1,20,000. Saving = 2,25,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹1,05,000, option C. Option A forgets to subtract the voucher cost. Option D is the whole loss without recovery, not the saving.

bdm-w12-q6.question: One B2B account of fictional IT services firm 'Sankalp Tech' brings ₹40 lakh of revenue and ₹12 lakh of margin a year. After a major outage, the probability of contract renewal without recovery is 50%. A ₹3 lakh recovery program (service credit + dedicated engineer + root-cause report) raises the renewal probability to 80%. Based on next year's expected margin, should it run the recovery program?
options: Yes; expected margin is ₹9 lakh higher
No; renewal is still not certain, so the ₹3 lakh is wasted
Yes; expected margin is ₹3.6 lakh higher
bdm-w12-q6.explanation: Without recovery: 50% × 12 = ₹6 lakh. With recovery: 80% × 12 − 3 = ₹6.6 lakh. The difference is ₹0.6 lakh = ₹60,000, option A. Option B uses revenue instead of margin (30% × 40 − 3). Option D forgets the ₹3 lakh recovery cost. Option C demands a 'certain' outcome instead of expected value; raising the probability is the value.

bdm-w1-q7.question: Kavya, founder of fictional 'Kavya Designs', left a job paying ₹15 lakh per year to start her own studio. The studio's first-year accounting profit (revenue − cash expenses) is ₹10 lakh. If the job was the next best alternative, what is the economic profit once the implicit cost is included?
bdm-w1-q7.explanation: Economic profit = accounting profit − implicit cost = ₹10 lakh − ₹15 lakh (salary given up) = −₹5 lakh, option B. Option A forgets the implicit cost; the studio shows a cash profit, but Kavya could have earned more in the job. Option C adds the implicit cost instead of subtracting it, and option D flips the sign of the right numbers.

bdm-w1-q8.question: Fictional 'Nimbu Juice Bar' is deciding whether to launch a new flavour next month. Which of these items is a sunk cost for this decision?
options: Fruits that will be bought for the new flavour
Expected extra revenue from the new flavour
Last month's survey fee that has been paid
Extra staff hours needed for the new flavour
bdm-w1-q8.explanation: The survey fee is already spent and won't come back whether or not they launch, so it is a sunk cost, option C. Options A and D are future incremental costs that arise only if they launch, and option B is future incremental revenue; all three are relevant to the decision.

bdm-w1-q9.question: Data from fictional 'Chai Point Express' shows 400 cups per day with 4 staff members and 460 cups per day with 5 staff members. What is the marginal product of the fifth staff member?
bdm-w1-q9.explanation: Marginal product = difference in the cumulative numbers = 460 − 400 = 60 cups, option D. Option A is the average at 5 staff (460 ÷ 5 = 92) and option B the average at 4 staff (400 ÷ 4 = 100); average and marginal are different. Option C is total output, not the extra output.

bdm-w1-q10.question: Fictional 'Arjun' has ₹5 lakh of savings earning 7% per year in an FD, and he has a part-time job paying ₹4 lakh per year. He breaks the FD, puts the money into a food cart and also quits the job. What is the implicit cost of one year of the business?
bdm-w1-q10.explanation: Implicit cost = the return given up on his own resources: FD interest ₹5,00,000 × 7% = ₹35,000 + salary given up ₹4,00,000 = ₹4,35,000, option A. Adding is right here because money and time are two separate resources that both went into the business. Option B forgets the return on money and option D the time. Option C adds the full ₹5 lakh principal, although only its return was given up.

bdm-w1-q11.question: The fictional 'Kagaz Prints' factory has spare capacity. A notebook's normal price is ₹25 and its average cost is ₹20 per notebook (including ₹8 per unit of allocated fixed cost; the rest is variable). A school wants 2,000 notebooks at ₹15 each; there is no effect on other sales. What will this order do to profit?
bdm-w1-q11.explanation: Variable cost = ₹20 − ₹8 = ₹12 per notebook. The fixed cost stays the same with or without the order. Extra profit = 2,000 × (₹15 − ₹12) = ₹6,000, option C. Option A is the trap of comparing with the ₹20 average cost (2,000 × −₹5). Option B treats the whole ₹30,000 revenue as profit and forgets the costs.

bdm-w1-q12.question: Fictional 'Bindu Insurance' is hiring telecallers. Monthly policies by number of callers: 1: 60, 2: 110, 3: 150, 4: 180, 5: 200, 6: 210. Each policy gives ₹600 contribution and each caller costs ₹20,000 per month. ₹50,000 has already been spent on office setup. How many callers should it keep to maximise profit?
bdm-w1-q12.explanation: Marginal policies: 60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10; MB = × ₹600 = ₹36,000, ₹30,000, ₹24,000, ₹18,000, ₹12,000, ₹6,000. MC = ₹20,000. The third caller's MB of ₹24,000 ≥ MC, the fourth's ₹18,000 < MC, so 3 callers, option B. Check: net contribution 16, 26, 30, 28, 20, 6 (₹ thousand), highest at 3. The ₹50,000 setup is sunk and changes no option. Option A is the average trap: at 5 callers the average 200 × 600 ÷ 5 = ₹24,000 per caller looks above cost, but the 4th and 5th callers' marginal benefit is lower. Option C is the 'it's only a small loss' mistake.

bdm-w1-q13.question: Fictional 'Phool Gifts' spends on ads in blocks of ₹10,000 across two channels, X and Y. Extra orders per block: X: first block 200, second 150, third 60; Y: first 180, second 120, third 90. Each order gives ₹80 contribution. The budget is up to ₹30,000 (it need not all be spent). How should the blocks be placed to maximise profit?
options: 1 block on X + 2 blocks on Y
2 blocks on X + 1 block on Y
bdm-w1-q13.explanation: Each block's MB = extra orders × ₹80: X: ₹16,000, ₹12,000, ₹4,800; Y: ₹14,400, ₹9,600, ₹7,200. MC = ₹10,000. The blocks with MB ≥ MC are X1, Y1, X2, and all three fit in the budget. Net = (200 + 180 + 150) × 80 − 30,000 = ₹12,400, option D. Option B (Y2's MB of ₹9,600 < cost) gives ₹10,000, option C ₹6,000, and option A ₹2,800; option A is the 'X's first block is best, so put everything on X' trap, while X's third block is deep in diminishing returns.

bdm-w1-q14.question: Fictional 'Megh Travels' bought a bus for ₹30 lakh; its resale value today is ₹18 lakh. Option 1: run the bus for one more year, earning ₹5 lakh net operating cash, and sell it for ₹14 lakh at the end of the year. Option 2: sell it now for ₹18 lakh. Ignore discounting. What is the right decision?
options: Run it; Option 1 is better by ₹1 lakh
Sell; it avoids a ₹4 lakh fall in value
Run it; Option 1 is better by ₹5 lakh
Sell; running it won't recover the ₹30 lakh
bdm-w1-q14.explanation: The ₹30 lakh is sunk and the same in both options. Option 1 = ₹5 lakh + ₹14 lakh = ₹19 lakh; Option 2 = ₹18 lakh. Running it is better by ₹1 lakh, option A. The opportunity cost of running it is today's ₹18 lakh resale. Option B looks only at the fall in resale value (₹4 lakh) and forgets the ₹5 lakh operating cash. Option C ignores the opportunity cost (the fall in resale). Option D is the sunk cost fallacy.

bdm-w1-q15.question: Fictional 'Dhoop Solar Lamps' has these daily total costs (₹) by output: 100 units: 30,000; 200: 52,000; 300: 76,000; 400: 1,04,000; 500: 1,40,000. Each lamp sells for ₹300 however many are made. Output can change only in steps of 100. What daily output maximises profit?
bdm-w1-q15.explanation: Marginal cost per unit for each 100-unit step: 220, 240, 280, 360. The price is ₹300, so expand while MC ≤ ₹300: up to 400 (280); at 500 it is 360 > 300. Profit: 0, 8,000, 14,000, 16,000, 10,000, highest at 400, option B. Option A is the output where average cost is lowest (76,000 ÷ 300 ≈ ₹253); that is the average trap, because units 301 to 400 have an MC of ₹280, still below the price. Option C maximises revenue, not profit.

bdm-w2-q7.question: Fictional 'Garam Chai Co.' cuts the price of its tea from ₹15 to ₹12 and, with everything else the same, cup sales rise. What is this on the demand curve?
options: A right shift of the demand curve
A left shift of the supply curve
A left shift of the demand curve
A movement along the demand curve
bdm-w2-q7.explanation: When the product's own price changes, quantity demanded moves along the curve; the curve doesn't shift, option D. The right shift in option A would happen if some other factor (income, taste, a complement's price) changed. Options B and C don't describe any change here.

bdm-w2-q8.question: When consumers' income rises by 10%, sales of fictional brand 'Saste Noodles' fall by 4% (everything else the same). What are the income elasticity and the type of good?
bdm-w2-q8.explanation: Income elasticity = %ΔQ ÷ %Δincome = −4% ÷ 10% = −0.4. Negative means demand falls as income rises, i.e. an inferior good, option A. Option B drops the sign. Option C takes the ratio upside down (10 ÷ 4). Option D gives the right number with the wrong type.

bdm-w2-q9.question: An essential medicine at a fictional pharmacy chain has a price elasticity of −0.3. Roughly what happens to quantity and revenue if the price is raised by 10%?
bdm-w2-q9.explanation: %ΔQ ≈ e × %ΔP = −0.3 × 10% = −3%. |e| < 1 (inelastic), so raising the price cuts quantity only a little and revenue rises, option C. Option A reads the elasticity as 3. Option B flips the sign. Option D has the right quantity but applies the elastic-demand revenue rule.

bdm-w2-q10.question: In a fictional city, demand for steel water bottles is Qd = 1,000 − 20P and supply is Qs = 30P − 250 (P in ₹). What are the equilibrium price and quantity?
bdm-w2-q10.explanation: At equilibrium Qd = Qs: 1,000 − 20P = 30P − 250, so 50P = 1,250 and P = ₹25. Q = 1,000 − 20 × 25 = 500 (from supply too: 750 − 250 = 500), option B. Option A is just a demand point at one price, not equilibrium. Option C has the right price but the wrong quantity, and option D doesn't come from the equations.

bdm-w2-q11.question: Fictional 'Raahi Bikes' raised its rental price from ₹40 to ₹50 per hour, and daily rentals fell from 1,800 to 1,400. Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity (absolute value), and what happened to revenue?
bdm-w2-q11.explanation: %ΔQ = −400 ÷ 1,600 = −25%; %ΔP = 10 ÷ 45 ≈ 22.2%. |e| = 25 ÷ 22.2 ≈ 1.13, elastic. Revenue fell from ₹72,000 (40 × 1,800) to ₹70,000 (50 × 1,400), option A. The 0.89 in options B and C comes from simple base-value percentages (22.2% ÷ 25%), not the midpoint method. Option D says revenue rises when price goes up under elastic demand, which is backwards.

bdm-w2-q12.question: An analyst at fictional 'Kesar Snacks' fitted this model on past data: ln Q = 8 − 1.5 ln P (constant-elasticity demand). If the price is raised by 10%, roughly how will total revenue change?
bdm-w2-q12.explanation: In this model the slope −1.5 is the elasticity (at every price). New Q = old Q × 1.1^(−1.5) ≈ 0.867 times (≈ −13.3%). Revenue = P × Q = 1.1 × 0.867 ≈ 0.953 times, i.e. about 4.7% lower, option D (quick check: +10% − 15% ≈ −5%). Option A takes the change in quantity as the change in revenue. Option B assumes a price rise lifts revenue under elastic demand (|e| = 1.5 > 1), which is backwards. Option C reads −1.5 as unit elastic.

bdm-w2-q13.question: Fictional 'Mitti Kulhad' faces weekly demand Q = 2,000 − 50P, and each kulhad has a variable cost of ₹10 (fixed costs are the same at every price). At which of these four prices is weekly profit highest?
bdm-w2-q13.explanation: Profit = (P − 10) × Q. P = 15: Q = 1,250, ₹6,250; P = 20: Q = 1,000, ₹10,000; P = 25: Q = 750, ₹11,250; P = 30: Q = 500, ₹10,000. Highest at ₹25, option C. Option A is the revenue-maximising price (a ÷ 2b = 2,000 ÷ 100 = ₹20), but variable cost isn't zero, so the profit-maximising price is above it. Option B is too high: the lost volume outweighs the margin gained.

bdm-w2-q14.question: In a fictional umbrella market, demand is Qd = 1,200 − 30P and supply is Qs = 20P − 200. When the monsoon arrives, demand rises by 150 units at every price (supply unchanged). What is the new equilibrium price, and if a platform holds the price at the old equilibrium, how big is the shortage?
bdm-w2-q14.explanation: Old equilibrium: 1,200 − 30P = 20P − 200, P = ₹28, Q = 360. New demand Qd = 1,350 − 30P: 1,350 − 30P = 20P − 200, P = ₹31 (Q = 420). If the price stays at ₹28, Qd = 1,350 − 840 = 510, Qs = 360, shortage = 150 units, option B. Option A takes the change in equilibrium quantity (420 − 360) instead of the shortage. Option C assumes a demand shift doesn't move the price.

bdm-w2-q15.question: Fictional tea brand 'Neel Giri' sells 5,000 packets a week at ₹120 each. Its cross-price elasticity of demand with respect to the price of competitor 'Pahadi Leaf' is +0.8. Pahadi Leaf cuts its price by 15% and Neel Giri keeps its price the same. Roughly what happens to Neel Giri's weekly revenue?
bdm-w2-q15.explanation: %ΔQ(Neel Giri) = +0.8 × (−15%) = −12%. New sales = 5,000 × 0.88 = 4,400 packets; revenue goes from ₹6,00,000 to ₹5,28,000, i.e. ₹72,000 lower, option C. Positive cross elasticity = substitutes, so when the competitor gets cheaper Neel Giri's sales fall; option A flips the sign (as if they were complements). Option B forgets the elasticity and applies the full 15%, and option D uses 15 ÷ 0.8 = 18.75%.

bdm-w3-q7.question: At fictional salon 'Roop Studio', a haircut is only 'produced' while the customer sits in the chair; the stylist and the customer are both part of the process at the same time. Which property of services does this show?
bdm-w3-q7.explanation: Production and consumption happen together, with the customer as part of the process: that is inseparability, option C. Option A (perishability) is about unused capacity that can't be sold tomorrow. Option B (intangibility) is about not being able to touch a service, and option D (heterogeneity) about quality varying each time.

bdm-w3-q8.question: At fictional school chain 'Gyan Deep', the principal chose a new attendance app. But the trust's rule is that any spend above ₹5 lakh is authorised by the finance committee, and the committee signed off this spend. What is the finance committee's role in the buying centre?
bdm-w3-q8.explanation: Whoever authorises the final decision is the approver, option B. The decider (option A) here is the principal who chose the app. A gatekeeper (option C) controls the flow of information, and an initiator (option D) is the first to recognise the need.

bdm-w3-q9.question: Fictional restaurant chain 'Swaad' has always bought from its existing vegetable supplier. Now it wants organic grade and new price terms, so it has asked 2 more suppliers for quotes. Which buying situation is this?
bdm-w3-q9.explanation: The category is familiar but the specs and terms are changing and some research (new quotes) is happening: a modified rebuy, option A. A straight rebuy (option B) would be a routine reorder without review. A new task (option C) is a first-time purchase. Option D isn't a buying situation; it is a concept about B2B demand.

bdm-w3-q10.question: At fictional company 'Neer Pumps', a new rule says that every purchase above ₹10 lakh will now be made by the head office's central procurement team rather than by each plant. At which level of organisational buying behaviour is this factor?
bdm-w3-q10.explanation: The company's own policy and purchase process (centralised vs decentralised buying) is an organisational factor, option D. Environmental factors (option A) are outside ones such as the economy or regulation. Option B is about authority and persuasion within the buying team, and option C about each member's personal traits.

bdm-w3-q11.question: A B2B account of fictional packaging vendor 'Dabba Solutions' brings ₹50 lakh revenue a year at a 30% gross margin, and the relationship is expected to last 4 years. Ignoring discounting, what is the account's value?
bdm-w3-q11.explanation: Annual margin = ₹50 lakh × 30% = ₹15 lakh; margin over 4 years = ₹15 lakh × 4 = ₹60 lakh, option B. Option A uses revenue × 4 instead of margin. Option C is just one year of margin, and option D one year of revenue; both forget the length of the relationship.

bdm-w3-q12.question: At the end of each month a fictional distributor sets inventory to 1.5 times next month's forecast (forecast = this month's sales), and orders arrive immediately. Until now sales were 2,000 units a month, inventory 3,000 and orders 2,000 units. In Month 1 sales rise to 2,400, and in Month 2 they return to 2,000. How much does the distributor order in each month?
bdm-w3-q12.explanation: Month 1: 3,000 − 2,400 = 600 left; target 1.5 × 2,400 = 3,600; order = 3,000 (sales +20%, orders +50%). Month 2: 3,600 − 2,000 = 1,600 left; target 1.5 × 2,000 = 3,000; order = 1,400. Option C. This is the bullwhip effect: a small swing in consumer demand grows larger upstream. Option A assumes orders = sales. Option B forgets to bring the inventory target back down. Option D orders the full target in Month 1, forgetting the stock left over.

bdm-w3-q13.question: Fictional IT vendor 'Sampark Systems' has two accounts. Account P: ₹80 lakh revenue per year, 15% margin, 50% probability of staying each year. Account Q: ₹40 lakh revenue per year, 25% margin, 80% retention probability. The first year's margin is certain; ignore discounting. Based on expected total margin, which account should get priority?
options: Account Q; expected total margin ₹50 lakh
Account P; expected total margin ₹160 lakh
Account Q; expected total margin ₹200 lakh
Account P; expected total margin ₹24 lakh
bdm-w3-q13.explanation: Expected total margin = m ÷ (1 − r). P: m = ₹12 lakh, 12 ÷ 0.5 = ₹24 lakh. Q: m = ₹10 lakh, 10 ÷ 0.2 = ₹50 lakh. Q is worth more than double, option A. Options B and C apply the formula to revenue instead of margin (80 ÷ 0.5, 40 ÷ 0.2). Option D gets P's value right but picks it without comparing with Q; bigger revenue doesn't necessarily mean bigger account value.

bdm-w3-q14.question: Fictional 'Kshitij Motors' is buying new CAD software. The design engineers raised the problem and will use the software; the IT manager writes the compatibility specs; the plant head picks the final vendor; and the MD's assistant decides which vendors' calls and emails get through. Which mapping is correct?
options: Engineers: initiator + user; IT manager: decider; assistant: buyer
Engineers: user; IT manager: influencer; plant head: approver
Engineers: initiator; IT manager: gatekeeper; plant head: decider
Engineers: initiator + user; IT manager: influencer; assistant: gatekeeper
bdm-w3-q14.explanation: The engineers recognised the need (initiator) and will use it (user); one person can hold several roles. The IT manager shapes the evaluation through specs (influencer). The plant head is the decider, and the assistant who controls the information flow is the gatekeeper. Option D is correct. Option A makes the IT manager the decider. Option B calls the plant head the approver, though he makes the final choice. Option C mistakes the IT manager for the gatekeeper.

bdm-w3-q15.question: Fictional hotel 'Pahadi Nook' has 40 rooms at ₹4,000 per night; on off-season weekdays only 16 sell. Each occupied room has a variable cost of ₹800. The manager starts a ₹2,500 'last-minute' rate: it brings 14 new guests who otherwise wouldn't come, but 3 of the original 16 guests also switch from paying ₹4,000 to ₹2,500. What is the net effect on one night's contribution?
bdm-w3-q15.explanation: An empty room is perishable; if it isn't sold tonight its value is zero, so the new guests' marginal contribution = 14 × (₹2,500 − ₹800) = ₹23,800. But 3 existing guests now pay ₹1,500 less: −₹4,500. Net = +₹19,300, option D. Option A forgets this cannibalisation. Option B forgets both variable cost and cannibalisation (14 × ₹2,500). Option C subtracts the cannibalisation but forgets variable cost.

bdm-w4-q7.question: Cell B2 contains the formula `=A$1*2`. The formula is copied down from B2 to B5. What is the formula in B5?
bdm-w4-q7.explanation: Copying down shifts only rows, not columns. In `A$1` row 1 is locked and column A doesn't change, so the formula stays `=A$1*2`, option A. Option C ignores the `$` and shifts the row. Option B shifts the locked row too. Option D shifts the column, which never happens when copying down.

bdm-w4-q8.question: In a sales sheet, column B holds Region and column D holds Amount (rows 2 to 20). Which formula correctly gives the total amount for the 'South' region?
bdm-w4-q8.explanation: `SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range)`: the criteria range (Region, B) comes first and the range to add (Amount, D) last, option D. Option A swaps the ranges. Option B uses the `SUMIFS` order (sum_range first) but with the ranges swapped, so it would try to add the Region column. Option C only counts the South rows, not their total.

bdm-w4-q9.question: In a sheet at fictional 'Lata Traders', some values in the Amount column have been stored as text instead of numbers (a left-aligned '4500' in the cell). What happens to `=SUM(...)` on this column?
options: Text values are skipped; total comes out low
Text is converted to numbers automatically
It totals only the text cells
bdm-w4-q9.explanation: `SUM` ignores text cells in a range without any error, so the total comes out quietly low, option B. That is why data cleaning is needed before a pivot or a total. Option A is wrong because no error appears; that is exactly what makes this mistake dangerous. Option C assumes an automatic conversion, which doesn't happen in a `SUM` range.

bdm-w4-q10.question: On the sheet of fictional 'Kalam Stationers' (see the code), what does `=COUNTIFS(B2:B8, "North", C2:C8, "Pen*")` return?
bdm-w4-q10.explanation: `Pen*` means any text starting with 'Pen' (zero or more characters), and text matching is case-insensitive. North + Pen*: N01 (Pencil), N03 (Pen Drive), N04 (north, Pen) = 3, option C. Option A drops 'north' because of its case. Option B ignores the wildcard and counts only an exact 'Pen'. Option D forgets the Region condition and counts every Pen*.

bdm-w4-q11.question: On the product table below, what does `=VLOOKUP("P104", A2:D6, 3, FALSE)` return?
bdm-w4-q11.explanation: FALSE = exact match, so unsorted IDs are not a problem. 'P104' is found in row 4; col_index 3 = the third column of table A:D (C) = 'Kitchen', option D. Option A is the trap of counting columns from B (Name), and option B is column 4 (Price). Option C would appear only if the ID weren't in the table.

bdm-w4-q12.question: An analyst wrote this formula for customer tiers and copied it over five values in column B (3000, 25000, 60000, 12000, 50000): `=IF(B2>=5000,"Silver",IF(B2>=20000,"Gold",IF(B2>=50000,"Platinum","Basic")))`. How many customers get 'Gold' or 'Platinum'?
bdm-w4-q12.explanation: A nested IF is checked top to bottom and stops at the first true condition. Every value ≥ 5000 (25000, 60000, 12000, 50000) becomes 'Silver' at the very first test; 3000 fails every test and gets 'Basic'. Nobody gets Gold or Platinum, option A. With slabs, the biggest condition should come first. Option B is the count the correct order (Platinum → Gold → Silver) would give (25000 Gold; 60000, 50000 Platinum). Options C and D are partial-tracing mistakes.

bdm-w4-q13.question: On the quarterly sales table of fictional 'Sona Sweets' (see the code), the analyst wrote `=INDEX(B2:E5, MATCH("Q3", A1:A5, 0), 3)` to get the Q3 East number. What does the formula return?
bdm-w4-q13.explanation: The MATCH range A1:A5 starts at the header, so 'Q3' is at position 4 (Qtr = 1). But the INDEX range B2:E5 starts at row 2, so INDEX(B2:E5, 4, 3) = the third column (D, East) of row 5 (Q4) = 360, option B. This is an off-by-one mistake: the MATCH and INDEX ranges must start on the same row (A2:A5). Option A is the number the analyst wanted. Option C counts columns from A (South), and option D takes column 1 (North).

bdm-w4-q14.question: A pivot at fictional 'Megha Retail' shows average order value by region: North ₹4,000 (30 orders), South ₹6,000 (10 orders), East ₹5,500 (20 orders). The manager calls the simple average of the three averages the 'overall average'. What is the correct overall average order value?
bdm-w4-q14.explanation: Overall average = total amount ÷ total orders = (30 × 4,000 + 10 × 6,000 + 20 × 5,500) ÷ 60 = 2,90,000 ÷ 60 ≈ ₹4,833.33, option C. Option A is the simple average of the three averages, which weights every region equally although North has the most orders. Options B and D are also averages built without the order-count weights. The pivot's Grand Total average, computed from the raw rows, gives this weighted number.

bdm-w4-q15.question: In a price-growth grid (see the code), B2 has the formula `=$A2*(1+B$1)`, with base prices in column A and growth rates in row 1. The formula is copied into B2:D3. What is the value in cell D3?
bdm-w4-q15.explanation: From B2 to D3: 2 columns right, 1 row down. In `$A2` the column is locked and the row moves: `$A3`. In `B$1` the row is locked and the column moves: `D$1`. D3 = `=$A3*(1+D$1)` = 500 × 1.20 = 600, option B. Option A treats the row as locked and uses A2 (200 × 1.20). Option C uses column C's 10%, and option D assumes the growth stays stuck on column B (500 × 1.05).

bdm-w5-q7.question: Fictional 'Charu Textiles' has total assets of ₹90 lakh and total liabilities of ₹35 lakh. By the accounting equation, what is equity?
bdm-w5-q7.explanation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity, so Equity = ₹90 lakh − ₹35 lakh = ₹55 lakh, option B. Option A adds assets and liabilities. Options C and D just pick one side of the equation.

bdm-w5-q8.question: Which of these financial statements is a snapshot of the company on a specific date (such as 31 March) rather than over a whole period?
bdm-w5-q8.explanation: The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity on one date, i.e. a snapshot, option A. Option B (the income statement) and option C show performance over a period (the period's movie). Option D is also a month's flow, not a balance on a date.

bdm-w5-q9.question: On 31 March, fictional SaaS firm 'Sutra Cloud' signed a ₹36 lakh 3-year contract with a client. No invoice has been raised and no service delivered yet. Which metric does this ₹36 lakh belong to?
bdm-w5-q9.explanation: The value of a signed contract is bookings, option D. Option B is wrong because no invoice has been raised (billings = what was invoiced). Option A is wrong because revenue is earned as the service is delivered. Option C would arise if a cash advance had been received with the service still pending; here no cash came in and no invoice was raised.

bdm-w5-q10.question: Fictional 'Bela Foods' had opening retained earnings of ₹40 lakh. Net profit for the year was ₹18 lakh, and ₹6 lakh of dividends were paid to shareholders. What are closing retained earnings?
bdm-w5-q10.explanation: Closing retained earnings = opening + net profit − dividends = 40 + 18 − 6 = ₹52 lakh, option C. Option A forgets to subtract the dividend. Option B adds the dividend. Option D is only this year's (profit − dividend), forgetting the opening balance.

bdm-w5-q11.question: Fictional 'Tanvi Electronics' has this data for the year (₹ lakh): revenue 200, COGS 120, other operating expenses 30, depreciation 10, interest 8, tax rate 25%. What are EBIT and PAT?
bdm-w5-q11.explanation: Gross profit = 200 − 120 = 80; EBITDA = 80 − 30 = 50; EBIT = 50 − 10 = 40; PBT = 40 − 8 = 32; PAT = 32 × 0.75 = 24. Option C. Option A calls EBITDA the EBIT and PBT the PAT. Option B applies tax to EBIT and forgets interest (40 × 0.75). Option D mistakes PBT for EBIT.

bdm-w5-q12.question: On 1 September 2025, fictional ed-tech 'Rekha Learning' sold an 18-month training programme to a corporate client for ₹5,40,000 and received the full cash upfront. The service is delivered evenly each month, and the financial year ends on 31 March. What are FY 2025-26 revenue and deferred revenue on 31 March 2026?
bdm-w5-q12.explanation: Monthly revenue = ₹5,40,000 ÷ 18 = ₹30,000. September to March = 7 months, so FY revenue = ₹2,10,000, and the obligation for the remaining 11 months, ₹3,30,000, is deferred revenue (a liability), option B. Option A is the trap of dividing by 12 instead of 18 (₹45,000 × 7). Option C treats the cash received as revenue. Option D counts only 6 months, leaving out September.

bdm-w5-q13.question: Fictional marketplace 'Bazaar Ghar' has these yearly numbers: GMV of ₹30 crore for goods sold on behalf of sellers (as an agent), on which it earns 10% commission; direct sales from its own inventory (as principal) of ₹8 crore; and advertising fees from sellers of ₹1 crore. What is Bazaar Ghar's revenue?
bdm-w5-q13.explanation: In the agent business, revenue is only the commission: ₹30 crore × 10% = ₹3 crore. When it sells its own inventory the company is the seller, so the full ₹8 crore sale is revenue. Ad fees are also its own fees: ₹1 crore. Total = 3 + 8 + 1 = ₹12 crore, option D. Option A treats the whole GMV as revenue. Option B forgets its own direct sales. Option C adds GMV and direct sales, dropping both the fees and the commission logic.

bdm-w5-q14.question: Fictional 'Sahyog Traders' starts with Assets ₹100 lakh = Liabilities ₹40 lakh + Equity ₹60 lakh. Then: (i) takes a ₹20 lakh bank loan; (ii) buys ₹15 lakh of goods on credit; (iii) sells goods costing ₹6 lakh for ₹10 lakh cash; (iv) pays ₹3 lakh rent in cash; (v) repays ₹5 lakh of the loan. What are total assets and equity now?
bdm-w5-q14.explanation: Assets: 100 + 20 (cash) + 15 (inventory) + 10 − 6 (cash in, inventory out) − 3 (rent) − 5 (repayment) = 131. Liabilities: 40 + 20 + 15 − 5 = 70. Equity: 60 + 4 (gross profit) − 3 (rent expense) = 61. Check: 70 + 61 = 131, option A. Option B treats the whole ₹10 lakh sale as profit (forgetting the ₹6 lakh of inventory leaving). Option C treats the loan repayment as an expense; a repayment only reduces cash and the liability. Option D subtracts the repayment twice.

bdm-w5-q15.question: The financial year of fictional 'Jyoti Packaging' ends on 31 March. (i) The ₹60,000 bill for March electricity arrived in April and was paid in April. (ii) On 1 January it paid a 12-month insurance premium of ₹1,20,000 in cash. A cash-basis dashboard shows the FY expense for these two as ₹1,20,000. On an accrual basis, what is the FY expense for these two items?
bdm-w5-q15.explanation: Matching: an expense belongs to the period in which the service was used. March electricity belongs to this FY even though the cash left in April: ₹60,000. Only 3 of the 12 insurance months (Jan–Mar) fall in this FY: ₹1,20,000 × 3 ÷ 12 = ₹30,000; the other ₹90,000 is a prepaid asset for next year. Total = ₹90,000, option A. Option C is the cash-basis number. Option B expenses both in full. Option D takes only the insurance part and forgets the electricity accrual.

bdm-w6-q7.question: Under the modern classification (asset, liability, equity, revenue, expense), which of these accounts increases with a credit?
bdm-w6-q7.explanation: A credit increases liabilities, equity and revenue, so sales revenue, option C. Options A and D are assets and option B is an expense; all three increase with a debit.

bdm-w6-q8.question: Fictional 'Pushp Foods' took a ₹10 lakh term loan from a bank. Under which activity will this ₹10 lakh inflow appear in the cash flow statement?
bdm-w6-q8.explanation: Loans, share issues and dividends are financing activities, option D. Option A is for day-to-day business cash (customers, suppliers, salaries). Option B is for buying or selling assets. Option C is wrong because real cash came in from the bank.

bdm-w6-q9.question: When purchase prices keep rising, how do COGS and profit under the FIFO method compare with the weighted average method?
options: COGS lower, closing inventory also lower
bdm-w6-q9.explanation: FIFO assumes the earlier (cheaper) units are sold first, so COGS is lower and profit higher, option A; the newer, costlier units stay in closing inventory, so it is higher. Option B is the reverse. Option D has COGS right but the wrong direction for closing inventory.

bdm-w6-q10.question: Fictional 'Vaibhav Prints' bought a ₹10 lakh printing machine: useful life 6 years, residual value ₹1 lakh, straight-line depreciation. What is the machine's carrying amount after 2 years?
bdm-w6-q10.explanation: Annual depreciation = (₹10 lakh − ₹1 lakh) ÷ 6 = ₹1.5 lakh. After 2 years = 10 − 3 = ₹7 lakh, option B. Option A forgets to subtract the residual value (10 ÷ 6 per year). Option C subtracts only one year of depreciation. Option D assumes ₹2 lakh per year.

bdm-w6-q11.question: Fictional 'Deepak Lights' had opening inventory of 100 bulbs @ ₹50, then bought 200 bulbs @ ₹60. It sold 180 bulbs in the period. Under FIFO, what are COGS and closing inventory?
bdm-w6-q11.explanation: FIFO: first the old 100 @ ₹50 = ₹5,000, then 80 @ ₹60 = ₹4,800; COGS = ₹9,800. The remaining 120 @ ₹60 = ₹7,200, option B. Check: 9,800 + 7,200 = 17,000 = total cost. Option A is LIFO (newest first), which Ind AS 2 doesn't even allow. Option C is weighted average (₹56.67 per bulb). Option D values every unit at ₹50.

bdm-w6-q12.question: Fictional 'Ganga Mills' bought a ₹10 lakh machine and depreciates it by the 20% written-down value (WDV) method. What are the third year's depreciation and the carrying amount at the end of the third year?
bdm-w6-q12.explanation: WDV = rate × opening carrying amount. Year 1: 20% × 10 = 2, closing 8. Year 2: 20% × 8 = 1.6, closing 6.4. Year 3: 20% × 6.4 = 1.28, closing 5.12. Option C. Option A applies 20% to the original cost each year (like SLM). Option B gives the second year's numbers. Option D has the right depreciation but gives the third year's opening amount, not the closing one.

bdm-w6-q13.question: Fictional 'Aakar Hardware' has a net profit of ₹12 lakh for the year and depreciation of ₹3 lakh. Working capital: trade receivables fell by ₹2 lakh, inventory rose by ₹4 lakh, trade payables fell by ₹1 lakh. What is operating cash flow (CFO) by the indirect method?
bdm-w6-q13.explanation: CFO = 12 + 3 (add back depreciation) + 2 (receivables fell, cash came in) − 4 (inventory rose, cash tied up) − 1 (payables fell, cash went out) = ₹12 lakh, option A. Option B reverses every working capital sign (12 + 3 − 2 + 4 + 1). Option C forgets to add back depreciation. Option D also subtracts the fall in receivables (12 + 3 − 2 − 4 − 1).

bdm-w6-q14.question: In one month fictional 'Kumud Traders': (1) paid an old ₹2 lakh supplier payable in cash; (2) sold goods costing ₹2 lakh for ₹3 lakh on credit; (3) recorded ₹0.5 lakh depreciation on shop equipment; (4) bought a new ₹4 lakh machine for cash. What are the month's profit, operating cash flow and investing cash flow?
options: Profit ₹1 lakh; CFO −₹2 lakh; investing −₹4 lakh
Profit ₹0.5 lakh; CFO −₹2.5 lakh; investing −₹4 lakh
Profit ₹0.5 lakh; CFO ₹1 lakh; investing −₹4 lakh
Profit ₹0.5 lakh; CFO −₹2 lakh; investing −₹4 lakh
bdm-w6-q14.explanation: Profit = 3 − 2 (COGS) − 0.5 (depreciation) = ₹0.5 lakh. Operating cash: only the supplier payment, −₹2 lakh (the sale was on credit, depreciation is non-cash). The machine, −₹4 lakh, is investing. Option D. Indirect check: 0.5 + 0.5 − 3 (receivables) + 2 (inventory fell) − 2 (payables fell) = −2. Option A forgets depreciation. Option B treats depreciation as a cash outflow. Option C treats the credit sale as cash.

bdm-w6-q15.question: Fictional 'Lalit Garments' (₹ lakh): opening inventory 80, purchases 300, revenue 450. At the year-end stock count, closing inventory was wrongly recorded as 70, while the correct figure is 60. What are the reported gross profit and the correct gross profit?
bdm-w6-q15.explanation: COGS = opening + purchases − closing. Reported: 80 + 300 − 70 = 310, gross profit = 450 − 310 = 140. Correct: 80 + 300 − 60 = 320, gross profit = 130. Overstating closing inventory by ₹10 lakh understates COGS by ₹10 lakh and overstates profit by ₹10 lakh, option C. Options A and D get the direction backwards. Option B gets the reported figure right but applies the error the wrong way to the correct profit.

bdm-w7-q7.question: Fictional 'Pavan Motors' has current assets of ₹90 crore and current liabilities of ₹60 crore. What is the current ratio?
