bdm-w7-q7.explanation: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5, option D. Option A takes the ratio upside down (60 ÷ 90). Option B is the difference (₹30 crore of working capital), not a ratio. Option C is a mistake like adding the two before dividing.

bdm-w7-q8.question: Which category of ratios does inventory turnover (COGS ÷ average inventory) belong to?
bdm-w7-q8.explanation: Inventory turnover shows how quickly inventory turns into COGS (and then cash); it is an efficiency / activity ratio, option B. Option A is the ability to pay short-term dues (current, quick ratio). Option C is long-term debt and coverage, and option D the share-price ratios (P/E, P/B).

bdm-w7-q9.question: Fictional 'Hira Chemicals' has EBIT of ₹45 crore and interest expense of ₹9 crore. What is the interest coverage ratio?
bdm-w7-q9.explanation: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest = 45 ÷ 9 = 5, option C. Option A is the ratio upside down. Option B subtracts interest from EBIT first ((45 − 9) ÷ 9); coverage is measured on EBIT itself. Option D is just the difference (45 − 9).

bdm-w7-q10.question: Fictional 'Kanchan Pharma' (₹ crore): current assets 200 (including inventories of 80 and prepaid expenses of 10), current liabilities 125. What is the quick ratio?
bdm-w7-q10.explanation: Quick ratio = (current assets − inventories − prepaid expenses) ÷ current liabilities = (200 − 80 − 10) ÷ 125 = 110 ÷ 125 = 0.88, option A. Option B removes only inventory and forgets prepaid (120 ÷ 125). Option C is the current ratio. Option D uses inventory itself as the numerator (80 ÷ 125).

bdm-w7-q11.question: Fictional distributor 'Amrit Agencies' has yearly revenue of ₹540 crore, COGS of ₹360 crore and closing trade receivables of ₹72 crore. What are receivables days (DSO, 365 days)?
bdm-w7-q11.explanation: DSO = receivables ÷ revenue × 365 = 72 ÷ 540 × 365 ≈ 48.7 days, option A. Option B is receivables turnover (540 ÷ 72), not days. Option C forgets to multiply by 365. Option D uses COGS instead of revenue (72 ÷ 360 × 365); receivables arise at selling price, so they are compared with revenue.

bdm-w7-q12.question: Fictional retailer 'Sarita Mart' has revenue of ₹600 crore, a net profit margin of 6%, average total assets of ₹400 crore and average equity of ₹200 crore. What are ROA and ROE?
bdm-w7-q12.explanation: PAT = 600 × 6% = ₹36 crore. ROA = net margin × asset turnover = 6% × (600 ÷ 400) = 9% (or 36 ÷ 400). ROE = 36 ÷ 200 = 18%; equity funds only half the assets and the rest is debt, so ROE is double ROA. Option D. Option A takes the net margin as ROA. Option B divides ROA by 2 instead of multiplying. Option C mistakes ROE for the net margin.

bdm-w7-q13.question: Fictional listed company 'Tulsi Agro Ltd' has PAT of ₹30 crore, out of which ₹2 crore of preference dividend is payable. The company has 4 crore equity shares and the share price is ₹105. What are EPS and the P/E ratio?
bdm-w7-q13.explanation: EPS = (PAT − preference dividend) ÷ equity shares = (30 − 2) ÷ 4 = ₹7. P/E = 105 ÷ 7 = 15, option B. Option A forgets to subtract the preference dividend (30 ÷ 4 = 7.5, 105 ÷ 7.5 = 14). Option C takes the ratio upside down (EPS ÷ price). Option D adds the preference dividend (32 ÷ 4).

bdm-w7-q14.question: Fictional 'Navya Fashions' has Q1 (3 months) revenue of ₹90 crore and trade receivables of ₹60 crore at the end of Q1. The analyst wants DSO on the annual definition (annualised revenue, 365 days). What is DSO?
bdm-w7-q14.explanation: Annualise the quarterly flow: ₹90 crore × 4 = ₹360 crore. DSO = 60 ÷ 360 × 365 ≈ 60.8 days, option C. Option A uses the quarterly revenue directly as if it were annual (60 ÷ 90 × 365), which makes DSO four times too big. Option B annualises by only 2, and option D by 12 (as if the revenue were monthly).

bdm-w7-q15.question: Two fictional companies each have EBIT of ₹20 crore and a 25% tax rate. 'Ojas Ltd' has no debt and equity of ₹100 crore. 'Prana Ltd' has ₹50 crore of debt at 10% interest and equity of ₹50 crore. What is each one's ROE (PAT ÷ equity)?
options: Ojas 15%, Prana 15%; leverage has no effect
bdm-w7-q15.explanation: Ojas: PAT = 20 × 0.75 = 15, ROE = 15 ÷ 100 = 15%. Prana: interest = 50 × 10% = 5, PBT = 15, PAT = 11.25, ROE = 11.25 ÷ 50 = 22.5%. Option D: leverage raised ROE because EBIT ÷ capital (20%) is above the interest rate (10%), but it raised risk too. Option A ignores the effect of leverage. Option B forgets Prana's interest (15 ÷ 50). Option C forgets tax (pre-tax numbers).

bdm-w8-q7.question: Fictional 'Prakash Electricals Ltd' has FY26 revenue of ₹300 crore and COGS of ₹216 crore (FY25: revenue ₹250 crore, COGS ₹175 crore). What is the FY26 gross margin?
bdm-w8-q7.explanation: Gross margin = (revenue − COGS) ÷ revenue = (300 − 216) ÷ 300 = 84 ÷ 300 = 28.0%, option A. Option B is the FY25 margin (75 ÷ 250); so the margin fell 2 points. Option C is COGS as a % of revenue. Option D divides gross profit by COGS (84 ÷ 216) instead of revenue.

bdm-w8-q8.question: A fictional company's CFO ÷ PAT ratio has stayed around 0.3 for three years in a row. In a case-study analysis, what is the best reading of this?
options: The company generates far more cash than profit
This is normal, because depreciation is non-cash
Much of the profit is stuck in working capital
It means PAT has been calculated wrongly
bdm-w8-q8.explanation: CFO ÷ PAT around 1 or above is seen as healthy (depreciation is added back). A steady 0.3 means the profit is on paper and the cash is stuck in working capital, option C; write questions on receivables ageing and inventory in the memo. Option A is the reverse. Option B is wrong because depreciation pushes CFO above PAT. Option D turns a red flag into a conclusion.

bdm-w8-q9.question: Fictional 'Vasu Steel' has FY26 operating cash flow (CFO) of ₹40 crore and capex of ₹55 crore. What is free cash flow?
bdm-w8-q9.explanation: FCF = CFO − capex = 40 − 55 = −₹15 crore, option B; this gap must be funded by debt, equity or the cash balance. Option A adds capex. Option C flips the sign. Option D forgets CFO.

bdm-w8-q10.question: Fictional 'Ratna Appliances' has these FY26 working capital days: DSO 50 days, DIO 70 days, DPO 45 days. What is the cash conversion cycle?
bdm-w8-q10.explanation: CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO = 50 + 70 − 45 = 75 days, option D: for every rupee of sales, cash stays tied up in the business this long. Option A adds DPO; supplier credit shortens the cash cycle. Option B flips the sign of DIO (50 − 70 + 45). Option C flips the sign of DSO (70 + 45 − 50).

bdm-w8-q11.question: The revenue of fictional 'Prakash Electricals Ltd' went from ₹250 crore in FY25 to ₹300 crore in FY26, and closing trade receivables from ₹40 crore to ₹66 crore. What is the best statement about the quality of growth?
options: Receivables grew 20% like revenue; this is normal growth
The growth in receivables is strengthening the cash position
Revenue grew fast, so DSO fell and collection improved
Receivables up 65%, DSO about 58 to 80 days; ask for ageing
bdm-w8-q11.explanation: Revenue growth = 50 ÷ 250 = 20%; receivables growth = 26 ÷ 40 = 65%. DSO went from 40 ÷ 250 × 365 ≈ 58.4 to 66 ÷ 300 × 365 ≈ 80.3 days. Receivables grew much faster than revenue, so the quality of growth is in question (looser credit?), option D; write it in the memo as a question and ask for ageing. Option A gets the receivables growth wrong. Option B is backwards: more receivables means cash tied up. Option C gets the direction of DSO backwards.

bdm-w8-q12.question: Data for fictional 'Prakash Electricals Ltd' is below (₹ crore), tax 25%. Simplification: CFO = PAT + depreciation − change in net working capital (receivables + inventory − payables). What are FY26 CFO and free cash flow (CFO − capex)?
bdm-w8-q12.explanation: FY26 EBIT = 300 − 216 − 45 − 12 = 27; PBT = 27 − 9 = 18; PAT = 13.5. Change in working capital = +26 (receivables) + 13 (inventory) − 6 (payables rose, saving cash) = 33. CFO = 13.5 + 12 − 33 = −7.5; FCF = −7.5 − 40 = −47.5, option A. Option B ignores working capital. Option C either forgets to add back depreciation or flips the payables sign (both give −19.5). Option D adds working capital instead of subtracting it.

bdm-w8-q13.question: Below is the data for fictional 'Prakash Electricals Ltd' (₹ crore), tax 25%. In FY25 the EBIT margin was 10.0% and the PAT margin 6.0%. What are the FY26 EBIT margin and PAT margin?
bdm-w8-q13.explanation: FY26: gross profit = 84; EBIT = 84 − 45 − 12 = 27, margin 27 ÷ 300 = 9.0%. PBT = 27 − 9 = 18; PAT = 13.5, margin 4.5%. Option C. Margin bridge: gross margin fell from 30% to 28%, and interest rose from 2% to 3% of revenue, so the PAT margin fell more than EBIT. Option A calls the PBT margin (18 ÷ 300) the PAT margin. Option B calls the EBITDA margin (39 ÷ 300) the EBIT margin. Option D forgets to subtract interest (27 × 0.75 ÷ 300).

bdm-w8-q14.question: Below is the data for fictional 'Prakash Electricals Ltd' (₹ crore). How did debt-equity (borrowings ÷ equity) and interest coverage (EBIT ÷ interest) change from FY25 to FY26?
bdm-w8-q14.explanation: D/E: from 50 ÷ 150 = 0.33 to 90 ÷ 160 ≈ 0.56. EBIT: FY25 = 250 − 175 − 40 − 10 = 25, FY26 = 27; coverage from 25 ÷ 5 = 5.0 to 27 ÷ 9 = 3.0. Option B: growth was funded by debt and coverage fell, which raises risk in a downturn. Option A subtracts interest from EBIT before computing coverage ((27 − 9) ÷ 9). Option C divides debt by (debt + equity), which isn't debt-equity. Option D uses PAT (13.5 ÷ 9) instead of EBIT.

bdm-w8-q15.question: Below is the data for fictional 'Prakash Electricals Ltd' (₹ crore). Using FY26 closing balances and 365 days, with DSO on revenue and DIO, DPO on COGS, what is the cash conversion cycle?
bdm-w8-q15.explanation: DSO = 66 ÷ 300 × 365 ≈ 80.3; DIO = 48 ÷ 216 × 365 ≈ 81.1; DPO = 36 ÷ 216 × 365 ≈ 60.8. CCC = 80.3 + 81.1 − 60.8 ≈ 100.6 days, option B. Option A forgets to subtract DPO. Option C adds DPO. Option D computes DIO and DPO on revenue too; inventory and payables are carried at cost, so they are compared with COGS.

bdm-w9-q7.question: Fictional 'Chandan Candles' has a fixed factory rent of ₹60,000 per month. Output rises from 1,000 to 2,000 candles per month (rent unchanged). How does the per-unit rent cost change?
bdm-w9-q7.explanation: Fixed cost per unit = ₹60,000 ÷ units: ₹60 at 1,000, ₹30 at 2,000, option B. Total fixed cost stays the same; per unit it falls as volume rises. Option C treats fixed cost per unit as constant like a variable cost. Options A and D get the direction backwards.

bdm-w9-q8.question: Fictional 'Mehndi Bags' sells a bag for ₹250; the variable cost is ₹150 per bag. What is the contribution margin ratio?
bdm-w9-q8.explanation: CM per unit = 250 − 150 = ₹100; CM ratio = 100 ÷ 250 = 40%, option D. Option A is variable cost as a % of price. Option B is just the variable cost. Option C divides CM by variable cost instead of price (100 ÷ 150).

bdm-w9-q9.question: Which of these reports is an example of management accounting rather than financial accounting?
options: Ind AS annual report sent to shareholders
Audited balance sheet given to a lender
Audited income statement for the tax filing
bdm-w9-q9.explanation: Management accounting serves internal decisions (pricing, product mix, make-or-buy) and has no fixed format, option A. Options B, C and D are reports made under rules for outside users (investors, lenders, tax), i.e. financial accounting.

bdm-w9-q10.question: Fictional 'Kesari Spices' has monthly fixed costs of ₹18 lakh and a contribution margin ratio of 30%. What is the break-even revenue?
bdm-w9-q10.explanation: Break-even revenue = fixed costs ÷ CM ratio = 18 ÷ 0.30 = ₹60 lakh, option C. Check: ₹60 lakh × 30% = ₹18 lakh of contribution = fixed costs. Option A multiplies (18 × 3). Option B divides by (1 − CM ratio), which is the variable cost ratio. Option D multiplies fixed costs by the CM ratio.

bdm-w9-q11.question: Fictional 'Neel Fans' forecasts sales of 2,500 fans this month, and its break-even is 2,000 fans. What is the margin of safety?
bdm-w9-q11.explanation: Margin of safety = (actual − break-even) ÷ actual = (2,500 − 2,000) ÷ 2,500 = 20%, option A: sales can fall up to 20% before a loss. Option B divides by break-even (500 ÷ 2,000). Option C is break-even as a % of actual (2,000 ÷ 2,500). Option D is actual ÷ break-even.

bdm-w9-q12.question: Fictional 'Usha Moulds' has a mixed maintenance cost. Lowest activity month: 1,200 machine hours, cost ₹50,400. Highest: 3,000 machine hours, cost ₹93,600. Using the high-low method, what is the estimated maintenance cost next month at 2,500 machine hours?
bdm-w9-q12.explanation: Variable rate = (93,600 − 50,400) ÷ (3,000 − 1,200) = 43,200 ÷ 1,800 = ₹24 per hour. Fixed = 50,400 − 24 × 1,200 = ₹21,600. At 2,500 hours = 21,600 + 24 × 2,500 = ₹81,600, option C. Option A uses the highest month's average cost per hour (₹31.2), which treats the fixed part as variable. Option B forgets the fixed part. Option D uses the lowest month's average (₹42 per hour).

bdm-w9-q13.question: Fictional 'Akshar Pens' sells a pen set for ₹800; variable cost is ₹500 per set, monthly fixed costs are ₹6 lakh, and it currently sells 3,000 sets a month. Marketing says cutting the price to ₹750 will raise volume by 25%. Should it cut the price?
bdm-w9-q13.explanation: Now: 3,000 × (800 − 500) − 6,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. After the price cut: 3,750 units × (750 − 500) = 9,37,500 − 6,00,000 = ₹3,37,500. Profit rises by ₹37,500, option D. Option A takes the change in revenue (₹24 lakh to ₹28.125 lakh) as profit. Option B looks only at the ₹50 lost on the original 3,000 units and forgets the contribution of the extra 750 units. Option C has the right number but the wrong direction.

bdm-w9-q14.question: Fictional 'Swara Speakers' sells a speaker for ₹2,000; variable cost is ₹1,200 per unit, monthly fixed costs are ₹30 lakh, and sales are 5,000 units a month. What is the degree of operating leverage (DOL), and if sales volume falls 15% (price and costs unchanged), what will EBIT be?
bdm-w9-q14.explanation: Contribution = 5,000 × 800 = ₹40 lakh; EBIT = 40 − 30 = ₹10 lakh; DOL = 40 ÷ 10 = 4. If sales fall 15%, EBIT falls 4 × 15% = 60%: ₹4 lakh. Check: 4,250 × 800 = ₹34 lakh − ₹30 lakh = ₹4 lakh, option B. Option A lets EBIT fall only 15%, forgetting operating leverage. Option C computes DOL as contribution ÷ fixed costs. Option D takes the 60% as what remains of EBIT rather than what is lost.

bdm-w9-q15.question: Fictional 'Dhanya Kitchenware' sells two products in a sales mix of 2 kadhais : 1 cooker. Kadhai: price ₹300, variable cost ₹180. Cooker: price ₹500, variable cost ₹260. Monthly fixed costs are ₹14,40,000. How many kadhais and cookers must it sell to break even at this mix?
bdm-w9-q15.explanation: CM: kadhai ₹120, cooker ₹240. The bundle (2 kadhais + 1 cooker) has CM = 2 × 120 + 240 = ₹480. Bundles = 14,40,000 ÷ 480 = 3,000, i.e. 6,000 kadhais and 3,000 cookers, option C. Check: 6,000 × 120 + 3,000 × 240 = ₹14,40,000. Option A applies the bundle count to each product, forgetting the 2 in the mix. Options D and B use the simple average CM (₹180) (8,000 units), which is wrong when the mix isn't equal.

bdm-w10-q7.question: After the proposal, a fictional payroll software sales rep asks: "Would you like to start implementation on 1 July or on 15 July?" Which closing technique is this?
bdm-w10-q7.explanation: Instead of 'yes or no', the customer is given two 'yes' options (which date): an alternative-choice close, option C. Option A is an opinion check ('will this approach work?'). Option B recaps the agreed benefits and asks for the next step. Option D is not a close; it is answering a concern.

bdm-w10-q8.question: A fictional billing software salesperson says: "This software has a module for automatic GST invoice generation." In the FAB framework, what is this statement?
bdm-w10-q8.explanation: It only says what the product has: a feature, option A. An advantage would say what it does ('invoices are created instantly'), and a benefit what the customer gains ('20 hours saved every month'). Option D is a step of SPIN questioning, not FAB.

bdm-w10-q9.question: Last quarter's funnel at fictional 'Disha CRM': 1,000 leads → 250 proposals → 50 wins. What is the proposal-to-win conversion rate?
bdm-w10-q9.explanation: Stage-to-stage conversion = wins ÷ proposals = 50 ÷ 250 = 20%, option D. Option A is the overall lead-to-win rate (50 ÷ 1,000). Option B is lead-to-proposal (250 ÷ 1,000). Option C takes the ratio upside down.

bdm-w10-q10.question: The sales team at fictional 'Megh ERP' has a historical win rate (by value) of 20% and a quarterly quota of ₹3 crore. How much pipeline coverage (value) is needed to make the quota realistic?
bdm-w10-q10.explanation: Required coverage ≈ 1 ÷ win rate = 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5 times; pipeline = 5 × ₹3 crore = ₹15 crore, option B. Option A just adds 20% to the quota. Option C is 20% of the quota. Option D assumes only 2 times coverage, the 'above quota is fine' mistake.

bdm-w10-q11.question: A customer of fictional procurement software says: "Your price is 20% higher than the competitor's." The rep listened carefully and said, "I understand that budget matters to you." Following the objection-handling process, what should the next step be?
options: Offer a 20% discount right away to save the deal
Clarify if the real concern is budget, value or scope
Do a summary close and send the contract at once
Email a case study and end the meeting
bdm-w10-q11.explanation: Process: listen → acknowledge → clarify → respond → confirm. The rep has listened and acknowledged; now he must clarify what the concern is, option B, and only then can the right response (TCO, ROI, scope comparison) be given. Option A gives a discount without showing value. Option C closes without resolving the concern. Option D responds without clarifying and also skips the confirm step.

bdm-w10-q12.question: Last quarter at fictional 'Kavach Security Software': 4,000 leads → 800 qualified → 240 meetings → 96 proposals → 24 wins. Next quarter it needs 36 wins, but marketing can supply at most 5,000 leads. The first three stage rates stay the same. What must the proposal-to-win rate become?
bdm-w10-q12.explanation: Rates: 800 ÷ 4,000 = 20%, 240 ÷ 800 = 30%, 96 ÷ 240 = 40%. From 5,000 leads, proposals = 5,000 × 0.20 × 0.30 × 0.40 = 120. Required proposal-to-win = 36 ÷ 120 = 30%, option D. Option A is the current rate, which would give only 30 wins. Option B assumes lead volume stays at 4,000 and computes 36 ÷ 96. Option C turns the number of wins into a percentage.

bdm-w10-q13.question: Fictional 'Pragati HR Cloud' has a quarterly quota of ₹250 lakh, and ₹60 lakh of deals have already closed this quarter. Open pipeline: 4 deals × ₹25 lakh at 'discovery' (probability 10%), 3 deals × ₹40 lakh at 'proposal' (40%), and 2 deals × ₹50 lakh at 'negotiation' (70%). What are the weighted forecast and the gap to quota?
bdm-w10-q13.explanation: Weighted pipeline = 4 × 25 × 0.10 + 3 × 40 × 0.40 + 2 × 50 × 0.70 = 10 + 48 + 70 = ₹128 lakh. Forecast = ₹60 lakh closed + ₹128 lakh = ₹188 lakh; gap = 250 − 188 = ₹62 lakh, option A. Option B adds the unweighted pipeline (100 + 120 + 100). Option C forgets the closed deals. Option D multiplies only one deal's value per stage by the probability, forgetting the number of deals.

bdm-w10-q14.question: The solution of fictional fleet-tracking vendor 'Gati Track' costs ₹20 lakh one-time + ₹5 lakh per year; the competitor's costs ₹12 lakh one-time + ₹8 lakh per year. The customer objects to price because the upfront cost is ₹8 lakh higher. After how many years does Gati Track's total cost fall below the competitor's, and how much is saved on 5-year TCO?
bdm-w10-q14.explanation: Total cost: Gati = 20 + 5t, competitor = 12 + 8t. They are equal when 3t = 8, t ≈ 2.67 years. 5-year TCO: Gati 20 + 25 = ₹45 lakh, competitor 12 + 40 = ₹52 lakh, a saving of ₹7 lakh, option C. Option A divides ₹8 lakh by the ₹5 lakh annual fee, though the yearly saving is ₹3 lakh. Option B takes 5 years of yearly savings (3 × 5) and forgets the ₹8 lakh upfront gap. Option D gets the break-even wrong.

bdm-w10-q15.question: Fictional 'Sutradhar Analytics' needs ₹3 crore of bookings next quarter. The average deal size is ₹12 lakh and the proposal-to-win rate is 30%. What is the minimum number of proposals it must send?
bdm-w10-q15.explanation: Wins = ₹300 lakh ÷ ₹12 lakh = 25. Proposals = 25 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 83.3, and half a proposal can't be sent, so at least 84, option D. Option A calls the number of wins the number of proposals. Option B multiplies instead of dividing (25 × 0.30). Option C assumes a 25% win rate.

bdm-w11-q7.question: A fictional vendor's minimum acceptable price (reservation price) is ₹60 lakh, and the buyer, based on its BATNA, will pay at most ₹55 lakh. Which statement is correct?
options: The deal should be done at ₹57.5 lakh
There is no ZOPA; there should be no deal
bdm-w11-q7.explanation: A ZOPA exists only if the seller's minimum is at or below the buyer's maximum. Here ₹60 lakh > ₹55 lakh, so there is no ZOPA; each side's BATNA is better, option D. Option A calls the gap a ZOPA. Option B picks a midpoint that is outside both reservation prices (too low for the seller, too high for the buyer).

bdm-w11-q8.question: At fictional company 'Ruchi Foods', Sales and Marketing were stuck on the definition of a 'qualified lead'. In the end they met halfway: one of Sales' conditions and one of Marketing's were dropped, and each side gave a little. Which conflict-handling style is this?
bdm-w11-q8.explanation: Both parties give up something and meet halfway: compromising, option C. In collaborating (option A) they jointly find a solution that fully meets both sides' needs. In option B the issue would be put off. In option D one team would fully accept the other's view.

bdm-w11-q9.question: At fictional 'Sagar Retail', who makes the final decision on the written definition of the 'active customer' metric when teams disagree?
bdm-w11-q9.explanation: The data owner decides the metric's definition, option B. The data steward (option A) looks after data quality and the pipeline but doesn't decide the definition. Option C is, under the DPDP Act, the person whose personal data it is. Option D is a buying-centre role, not a data-governance one.

bdm-w11-q10.question: Fictional hospital 'Jeevan Care' wants to buy an analytics tool. It has a competitor's quote of ₹28 lakh, which needs a separate ₹2 lakh for staff training (the other vendor includes training free). What is the hospital's reservation price (the most it will pay the other vendor)?
bdm-w11-q10.explanation: The hospital's BATNA is the competitor, whose full cost = ₹28 lakh + ₹2 lakh training = ₹30 lakh. Paying more than this is worse than the BATNA, so the reservation price is ₹30 lakh, option A. Option B forgets the switching (training) cost, which pushes the walk-away point too low. Option C subtracts the cost instead of adding it. Option D is only the training cost.

bdm-w11-q11.question: The team at fictional company 'Nayan Optics' has been negotiating with a vendor for 8 months. In the final meeting the vendor raised the price by 15%. The team says: "So much time and effort has gone in; sign it at any price now." Which negotiation trap is the team in?
bdm-w11-q11.explanation: Doing the deal 'at any price' because of time and effort already spent (sunk) is escalation of commitment, option C; the right move is to compare the new price with the BATNA. Option A is about the first number becoming an anchor. Option B is about gain vs loss presentation. Option D is about overpaying when an offer is accepted instantly.

bdm-w11-q12.question: Fictional buyer 'Arogya Labs' and vendor 'Rekha Instruments' are negotiating three issues. The points for each option are below (higher = better). Which package maximises the two parties' total points?
bdm-w11-q12.explanation: Joint points per issue: price ₹50 lakh = 10 vs ₹45 lakh = 9; 3 years = 9 vs 1 year = 6; 60 days = 8 vs 30 days = 5. Best = ₹50 lakh + 3 years + 60 days = 27, option B. The vendor cares more about price and contract length, the buyer about payment terms; logrolling gives each side its important issue. Option A is best for the buyer (17 + 6 = 23), option C for the vendor (5 + 19 = 24), and option D gives 23; these are fixed-pie outcomes.

bdm-w11-q13.question: Fictional vendor 'Kirti Data' has a delivery cost of ₹22 lakh on a project; without the deal the same team could earn ₹6 lakh profit on another project. Buyer 'Shree Malls' has a competitor's quote of ₹33 lakh, which needs a separate ₹2 lakh integration cost (not needed with Kirti). Kirti is insisting on ₹36 lakh. Which statement is correct?
options: ZOPA ₹28–35 lakh; at ₹36 lakh the buyer picks the rival
ZOPA ₹22–33 lakh; there should be no deal at ₹36 lakh
ZOPA ₹28–35 lakh; ₹36 lakh works for both sides
ZOPA ₹22–35 lakh; Kirti makes a loss at ₹36 lakh
bdm-w11-q13.explanation: Kirti's reservation price = ₹22 lakh + ₹6 lakh profit given up = ₹28 lakh. The buyer's = ₹33 lakh + ₹2 lakh = ₹35 lakh. ZOPA = ₹28–35 lakh. ₹36 lakh is above the buyer's maximum, so the buyer is better off with the competitor, option A. Options B and D forget the opportunity cost (₹6 lakh), and option B the integration cost too. Option C gets the ZOPA right but still treats ₹36 lakh as inside it.

bdm-w11-q14.question: Fictional vendor 'Anant Robotics' has a ₹32 lakh offer from a buyer. If this deal fails, its BATNA is another client: a 60% chance that client pays ₹40 lakh and a 40% chance only ₹25 lakh. Delivery cost is the same in both cases and Anant is risk-neutral. What is the right decision?
options: Accept; ₹32 lakh beats the ₹25 lakh worst case
Accept; ₹32 lakh is about the BATNA's ₹32.5 lakh average
Reject; the other client may pay ₹40 lakh
Reject; the expected BATNA of ₹34 lakh beats the offer
bdm-w11-q14.explanation: Expected BATNA = 0.6 × 40 + 0.4 × 25 = 24 + 10 = ₹34 lakh. For a risk-neutral vendor, ₹32 lakh is ₹2 lakh below the BATNA, so reject (or counter above ₹34 lakh), option D. Option A compares only with the worst case. Option B ignores the probabilities and takes the simple average ((40 + 25) ÷ 2). Option C looks only at the best case, which is overconfidence.

bdm-w11-q15.question: The base deal between fictional buyer 'Pankh Airlines' and vendor 'Vayu Analytics': ₹40 lakh, 1-year contract, 30-day payment. 60-day payment is worth ₹3 lakh to the buyer and costs the vendor ₹1 lakh. A 3-year contract is worth ₹5 lakh to the vendor and costs the buyer ₹2 lakh. By how much does total joint value rise if both changes are added to the package?
bdm-w11-q15.explanation: 60-day payment: buyer +3, vendor −1, net +2. 3-year contract: vendor +5, buyer −2, net +3. Total joint gain = ₹5 lakh, option B; this is integrative logrolling, and the price can be adjusted to split it between them. Option A adds gains and costs together. Option C adds only the gains and forgets the costs. Option D is just the sum of the costs.

bdm-w12-q7.question: Fictional payments app 'Nidhi Pay' was down for 3 hours and no payment could go through during that time. What type of service failure is this?
options: Unprompted bad behaviour by an employee
Failure to handle a customer request
bdm-w12-q7.explanation: The service's basic job (payment) didn't happen: a core service failure, option A. Option B is about front-line staff behaviour, and option C about ignoring a special request. Option D is not a failure type; it is a dimension for judging recovery.

bdm-w12-q8.question: Fictional airline 'Neel Gagan' gave a full refund for a cancelled flight, but the customer had to call 5 times and the refund took 3 weeks to arrive. Which justice dimension of the recovery is weak?
bdm-w12-q8.explanation: The outcome (a full refund) was fine, but the process was slow and difficult (repeated calls, a long wait): procedural justice is weak, option B. Option A is about the outcome, which was given in full here. Option C is about behaviour (politeness, empathy). Option D isn't a justice dimension.

bdm-w12-q9.question: Fictional hotel chain 'Aangan Stays' lets front-desk staff give compensation of up to ₹2,000 (a free meal, a room upgrade) without a manager's approval. Which concept is this an example of?
bdm-w12-q9.explanation: Letting the front line recover up to a limit without approval is employee empowerment, option C; it makes recovery faster. Option B is the outcome the customer gets, not the policy. Option A is about satisfaction rising after recovery. Option D is a B2B contract remedy.

bdm-w12-q10.question: A B2B client of fictional SaaS provider 'Megh Desk' pays ₹4,00,000 per month. SLA: no credit at monthly uptime of 99.5% or more; 10% credit from 99.0% up to below 99.5%; 20% credit below 99.0%. In a 30-day month total downtime was 250 minutes. How much service credit does the client get?
bdm-w12-q10.explanation: 30 days = 43,200 minutes. Uptime = 1 − 250 ÷ 43,200 ≈ 99.42%, which is between 99.0% and 99.5%, so a 10% credit = ₹40,000, option D. (Only 216 minutes of downtime were allowed for 99.5%.) Option A assumes the SLA wasn't breached. Option B applies the 20% slab. Option C takes a share of the fee in proportion to the downtime (pro-rata), which isn't the SLA rule.

bdm-w12-q11.question: In one month fictional appliance brand 'Garima Home' sold 50,000 units of a new mixer model and received 90 formal complaints. Research says only 3% of dissatisfied customers complain formally. What is the estimate of dissatisfied customers, and their share of buyers?
bdm-w12-q11.explanation: Dissatisfied ≈ complaints ÷ complaint rate = 90 ÷ 0.03 = 3,000; share = 3,000 ÷ 50,000 = 6%, option A. Option B treats the complaint count as the whole problem (the complaint-iceberg trap). Option C multiplies 90 by 30. Option D has the right count but the wrong percentage.

bdm-w12-q12.question: At fictional e-pharmacy 'Sehat Plus', 500 orders a month go late or wrong. Without recovery, 40% of these customers churn; with a recovery programme, only 15%. The programme costs ₹300 voucher + ₹100 handling per affected customer. Average customer lifetime value (margin) is ₹2,500. What is the programme's net benefit per month?
bdm-w12-q12.explanation: Loss without recovery = 500 × 40% × 2,500 = ₹5,00,000. With recovery, churn loss = 500 × 15% × 2,500 = ₹1,87,500 and cost = 500 × ₹400 = ₹2,00,000; total ₹3,87,500. Net benefit = ₹1,12,500, option D. Option A forgets the programme cost. Option B subtracts only the voucher and forgets handling. Option C compares the recovery cost with the remaining churn loss, when it should be compared with the loss avoided (₹3,12,500).

bdm-w12-q13.question: A B2B account of fictional IT firm 'Setu Infotech' brings ₹20 lakh margin per year. If it renews, there is a 40% chance the account expands with ₹5 lakh extra margin. After an outage, renewal probability without recovery is 60%; a ₹4 lakh recovery programme raises it to 85%. Based on next year's expected margin, should the programme be run?
bdm-w12-q13.explanation: Expected margin on renewal = 20 + 40% × 5 = ₹22 lakh. Without the programme: 60% × 22 = ₹13.2 lakh; with it: 85% × 22 = ₹18.7 lakh. Difference ₹5.5 lakh − ₹4 lakh cost = ₹1.5 lakh, option B. Option A forgets the expansion (25% × 20 − 4). Option C looks only at the cost. Option D forgets to subtract the programme cost. In B2B the real risk is exactly renewal and expansion.

bdm-w12-q14.question: Fictional food brand 'Swadesh Bites' received 60 complaints in a month. Only 5% of dissatisfied customers complain. Of those who complain, 20% churn after recovery; of those who don't, 50% quietly churn. Customer lifetime value is ₹2,000. What is the expected churn loss from this month's dissatisfied customers?
bdm-w12-q14.explanation: Dissatisfied = 60 ÷ 0.05 = 1,200; of these 60 complained and 1,140 stayed silent. Churn = 60 × 20% + 1,140 × 50% = 12 + 570 = 582. Loss = 582 × 2,000 = ₹11,64,000, option C. Option A is only the complainers' loss (the tip of the iceberg). Option B applies 50% to all 1,200 and forgets the effect of recovery. Option D forgets the complainers' loss.

bdm-w12-q15.question: The failure data of fictional grocery app 'Taaza Basket' shows two root causes. Cause X: 400 failures per month, 20% of those customers churn, the fix costs ₹1,50,000 per month. Cause Y: 150 failures per month, 50% churn, the fix costs ₹1,00,000 per month. CLV is ₹3,000 and a fix removes the failures completely. There is budget for only one fix. Which should it fix?
bdm-w12-q15.explanation: X: churn loss avoided = 400 × 20% × 3,000 = ₹2,40,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹90,000 net. Y: 150 × 50% × 3,000 = ₹2,25,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹1,25,000 net. Y is better, option A. Option B looks only at the failure count, not the churn rate or cost. Options C and D forget to subtract the cost of the fix; without the cost X looks better, which is the wrong conclusion.
